The sulfur mass loading of the electrode was about 1 mg cm −2 .
Electrochemical Measurements : The electrochemical properties of various electrolytes were evaluated in 2032-type coin cells (MTI Corporation).

Li-S coin cells were assembled inside the MBraun glovebox with the above sulfur cathode disc, Celgard 3501 separator (a polypropylene microporous membrane with hydrophilic coatings), Li chip, and selected electrolyte of 60 μL.

Then the cells were cycled on a Lanhe battery testing system (Wuhan Land Electronics Co., Ltd.) by using galvanostatic charge–discharge tests at 0.2 C rate where 1 C corresponded to a current density of 1.0 mA cm −2 .

The Li-S cell containing the 3 M LiTFSI electrolyte delivered relatively stable cycling with good capacity retention (71.9%) after 200 cycles, while the Li-S cell with the 3 M LiFSI electrolyte exhibited fast capacity decay and lasted only 33 cycles (Figure 1 a).

It is observed that the cell with the 3 M LiTFSI electrolyte showed higher capacity retention as well as higher polarization when compared with the cell containing the 3 M LiFSI electrolyte.
The CE of the cell with 3 M LiTFSI electrolyte was initially 101% and then slowly decreased to 96.6% after 200 cycles (Figure 1 b).

Interestingly, the CE for the cell with 3 M LiFSI electrolyte was slightly higher than that with 3 M LiTFSI electrolyte, which indicates that some side reactions may happen on the anode side between metallic Li and electrolyte during the discharge process and form degradation products that could not be reversibly oxidized back in the following charge process.
This behavior will lead to a CE of slightly larger than 100% as shown in the red line of Figure 1 b.

Figure S6 in the Supporting Information shows that the cell using 3 M LiTFSI/DOL-DME electrolyte exhibits a stable CE while the cell with the 3 M LiFSI/DOL-DME electrolyte exhibits a very large fl uctuation in CE that indicates an unstable anode/electrolyte interface.

The decreased stability is because the N–S bond in the FSI − anion is fairly weak and the scission of this bond leads to the formation of lithium sulfate (LiSO x ) in the presence of polysulfi de species.

In contrast, in the LiTFSI-based electrolyte, the lithium metal anode tends to react with polysulfi de to form lithium sulfi de (LiS x ), which is more reversible than LiSO x formed in the LiFSI-based electrolyte.

The high salt concentration electrolytes could minimize the side reactions between the Li metal and the polysulfi de species, effectively reduce the corrosion to the Li anode, and suppress Li dendrite formation.
Concentrated electrolytes tend to reduce the solubility of lithium polysulfi des due to the lack of available solvent molecules to partially solvate the Li + cations.

Interestingly, the CE for the cell with 3 M LiFSI electrolyte was slightly higher than that with 3 M LiTFSI electrolyte, which indicates that some side reactions may happen on the anode side between metallic Li and electrolyte during the discharge process and form degradation products that could not be reversibly oxidized back in the following charge process.

The higher polarization shown in the voltage profi les of Li-S cell using 3 M LiTFSI electrolyte comparing with those using 3 M LiFSI electrolyte should be attributed to the higher viscosity and lower conductivity of the 3 M LiTFSI electrolyte (Table S1 in the Supporting Information).
This thickness is comparable to those of passivation layers built up in 3 M LiTFSI/DOL-DME electrolyte after 200 cycles.
This observation is a clear indication that Li metal anodes degrade much faster in the electrolyte containing LiFSI salt.

Comparing Figure 2 a,b and Figure S3a,b in the Supporting Information, the Li metal anode cycled in the 1 M LiTFSI electrolyte is more loose and porous than those cycled in the concentrated electrolyte.
This is consistent with the previous report that the Li-S cells using high concentration electrolyte exhibit better cyclability when compared to those using low concentrations of electrolyte.
Therefore the sulfur-related product generated on the surface of the cycled Li metal anode in LiTFSIbased electrolyte is related to polysulfi de formation, which is reversible in Li-S batteries.
However, in a Li-S battery using an electrolyte with LiFSI salt, more reaction products formed on the surface of Li metal anode are lithium sulfate (LiSO x ) whose formation is not reversible.
In this case, the cell exhibits a poor cyclability as shown in the red line in Figure 1 a and also in Figure 1 d.

Because part of the reaction products (LiSO x ) formed during the discharge process cannot be decomposed during the charging process, the charge capacity of a Li-S battery is less than the discharge capacity when LiFSI salt is used in the electrolyte.
This behavior will lead to a CE of slightly larger than 100% as shown in the red line of Figure 1 b.
Generation of more irreversible products (LiSO x ) in LiFSI-based electrolyte also leads to thicker passivation layers as shown in Figure S2b in the Supporting Information.
The results from Figure 3 a,c indicate that F and N are much less stable in the FSI − anion than in TFSI − anion under the conditions utilized here.
In other words, the lower bond strengths of N S and F S in the FSI − anion favor the formation of sulfate SO 2 and F.

The increased impedance in the cell with 3 M LiFSI electrolyte is consistent with the results shown in Figure 2 b and Figure 3 that revealed the rapid growth of a passivation layer composed of insulating lithium sulfate (LiSOx).

Figure S6 in the Supporting Information shows that the cell using 3 M LiTFSI/DOL-DME electrolyte exhibits a stable CE while the cell with the 3 M LiFSI/DOL-DME electrolyte exhibits a very large fl uctuation in CE that indicates an unstable anode/electrolyte interface.

We also found that the solubility of polysulfi de in the 3 M LiFSI electrolyte is lower than in the 3 M LiTFSI electrolyte (Figure S7 in Supporting Information), suggesting that LiFSI may precipitate during battery operation when the amount of Li 2 S 8 increases above a certain critical level.
This phenomenon may also contribute to the low CE of Li-S batteries with the 3 M LiFSI electrolyte.
The fast motion of FSI − anion is consistent with the lower polarization noted in the Li-S cell using 3 M LiFSI-DOL/DME electrolyte (Figure 1 d).

However, the larger diffusion coeffi cient of FSI − anions may also accelerate their decomposition on the surface of Li metal anodes and lead to the formation of much more lithium sulfate (Li 2 SO x ).
This will accelerate the capacity fade of Li-S batteries as shown in Figure 1 . 3.
The continuous decomposition of the FSI − anions will lead to fast growth of passivation layers dominated by insulating lithium sulfate.
A broken C S bond in the TFSI − anion can in principle lead to the formation of lithium sulfi de (LiS x ) in the presence of polysulfi de species.
The higher diffusion coeffi cient of FSI − anions, corresponding to a weaker coordination by other solvent molecules, may accelerate their decomposition on the surfaces of Li metal anodes.

The fundamental differences in the bond strengths within the FSI − anions and the TFSI − anions in the presence of polysulfi de species lead to a large difference in the stability of anode-electrolyte interfaces and performance of the Li-S batteries.

A similar electrolyte with the same TTE content but slightly less LiTFSI, (MeCN)2.5−LiTFSI:TTE, enables S reduction kinetics that closely resemble those in the conventional electrolyte while maintaining the enhanced stability of polysulfide near the cathode surface.

Contrary to previous suggestions, Raman and NMR spectroscopy coupled with ab initio molecular dynamics simulations show that TTE coordinates to Li+ at the expense of MeCN coordination, thereby producing a higher content of free MeCN, a good polysulfide solvent, in the electrolyte.

The electrolytes containing a higher free MeCN content facilitate faster polysulfide formation kinetics during the electrochemical reduction of S in a Li−S cell likely as a result of the solvation power of the free MeCN.
Increased TTE content results in increased free MeCN that is then able to solubilize polysulfides at the cathode, likely facilitating faster S electroreduction kinetics.

Interestingly, although the kinetics of polysulfide formation is enhanced, the diffusion of the polysulfide into the bulk electrolyte is greatly reduced relative to the conventional electrolytes. ■EXPERIMENTAL SECTION Electrolyte Preparation.

Previous studies suggest that the kinetics of the S reduction are hindered by the poor solubility of intermediate polysulfides, although the formation of polysulfide intermediates is still observed.22 The cause of poor kinetics is suggested ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces Research Article DOI: 10.1021/acsami.6b11358 ACS Appl.
to arise from the inability of MeCN to act as a polysulfide solvent due to its coordination to Li.22 However, many other variables can have an effect on the CV.

For example, the activity of Li is different in the MeCN electrolytes compared to the conventional electrolyte due to the drastic change in concentration (1 M to nearly 4 M) and the viscosity of the MeCN electrolytes is much greater.22 The CV was also measured for the (MeCN)2.5−LiTFSI and (MeCN)2−LiTFSI electrolytes with addition of the TTE cosolvent.

This result is surprising because addition of TTE decreases the viscosity of the solvent from 138 cP in (MeCN)2−LiTFSI to 8.6 cP in (MeCN)2−LiTFSI:TTE = 1:122 which we would expect to enhance the kinetics of S reduction, resulting in a more positive reduction potential.

As a reference, the viscosity of the conventional electrolyte, 1 M LiTFSI in DOL/TEGDME, is ∼3 cP.43 Such an effect is observed for the second reduction peak, which is shifted to a more positive potential as a result of TTE addition.

The persistence of the Raman peak intensity associated with the short chain polysulfide suggests that the consumption and diffusion of polysulfide at 1.8 V (the second reduction peak) is not substantial.
Thus, the S3 •−is more stable near the cathode surface in the solvate electrolytes, with or without TTE, compared to the conventional DOL/TEGDME electrolyte.
We hypothesize the formation of free MeCN in the electrolyte will affect the S electrochemical reduction processes by enhancing the polysulfide solvating capability of the electrolyte.
In the absence of polysulfide solvating molecules, the S reduction pathway would be forced to follow a solid-state conversion reaction in lieu of forming soluble polysulfide intermediates.
Here, however, the formation of free MeCN as a result of TTE addition allows for the formation of soluble intermediates that facilitate reduction.
We observe the enhancement of the formation rate of the S3 •−in the (MeCN)x−LiTFSI:TTE electrolyte containing the highest free MeCN content.
Interestingly, although the S reduction kinetics are improved likely as a result of free MeCN content, the stability of polysulfides near the cathode surface is unaffected.
The persistence of polysulfide near the cathode surface could be a consequence of either limited solubility or the higher viscosity in this electrolyte.

The viscosity of the electrolytes with TTE at a volume ratio of 1:1 (8.6 cP)22 is similar to that of the electrolyte that enables fast diffusion, 1 M LiTFSI in DOL/TEGDME (3 cP),43 suggesting that the limited solubility of polysulfides in the solvate electrolytes is the cause for decreased diffusion.
Therefore, it is likely that MeCN is able to solubilize the polysulfides at the electrolyte/S interface only, thereby maintaining the intermediates near the electrode surface.
This behavior is likely to result in good cycling capability as the loss of active material is decreased.
The formation of free MeCN could have implications on other battery performance metrics such as rate capability and S8 utilization efficiency.
However, it is important to mention that free MeCN could also affect the Li deposition and dissolution reactions at the anode of the Li−S battery.
Because of these competing effects, it is difficult to deconvolute the possible benefits of free MeCN at the cathode with the possible detrimental effects at the anode.

Additionally, it is interesting to note that in the tetraglyme−LiTFSI solvate system, addition of hydrofluoroether to the solvate structure decreases the solubility of polysulfides.16 This is likely due to the stronger binding of the tetraglyme to Li+ as a result of the chelate effect.20 Strong tetraglyme coordination prevents the hydrofluoroether from displacing the bound solvent from the solvate structure.19 Therefore, both the choice of solvent that forms the solvate structure and the choice of cosolvent used to dilute the solvate play an important role in the behavior of the electrolyte with respect to the cycling of the Li−S cell.
TTE exchanges with MeCN more readily in the (MeCN)2.5−LiTFSI electrolyte resulting in higher free MeCN content.
The content of free MeCN likely facilitates polysulfide formation kinetics through enhanced local solvation effects.

Additionally, the coordination of MeCN to Li+ inhibits its reactivity with the Li metal.26 Utilizing the (MeCN)2−LiTFSI electrolyte in a Li−S battery results in high capacity and stable cycling relative to the lowconcentration, ethereal analogues.22 However, this behavior is only attainable when the hydrofluoroether 1,1,2,2,-tetrafluoroethyl 2,2,3,3-tetrafluoropropyl ether (TTE) is used to presumably reduce the viscosity of the electrolyte and increase the conductivity.22 The neat solvate electrolyte results in severe capacity fade.22 In addition to the TTE’s ability to reduce the electrolyte viscosity, the TTE also affects the SEI on the Li metal surface27−29 and could have an impact on the S reduction pathway.30 Fluorinated ethers have been shown to suppress the polysulfide shuttle,31 reduce self-discharge,32 and generally improve the Coulombic efficiency and cycle life.30 In order to understand the beneficial effects of adding TTE to the (MeCN)2−LiTFSI solvate electrolyte on sulfur electrochemistry, we evaluate the electrochemical behavior of the Li− S cell as TTE is added to both the (MeCN)2−LiTFSI solvate electrolyte and a similar electrolyte with slightly lower LiTFSI concentration, (MeCN)2.5−LiTFSI.

The quantity of free MeCN in the electrolyte is important when considering the functionality of the solvate electrolyte vs a Li metal anode as MeCN readily and exothermically decomposes on Li metal.58 Free MeCN, however, is not necessarily decomposed on the Li surface in the solvate electrolyte due to the formation of an SEI that prevents or limits MeCN decomposition.26 Due to changes in the electronic structure of the TFSI anion as a result of (MeCN)2−LiTFSI complexes, the TFSI is preferentially decomposed on the Li surface, resulting in an SEI that is mostly composed of inorganic, anion decomposition products.26 The SEI is believed to hinder the decomposition of any free MeCN.
Although MeCN may not decompose at the anode, consideration must be given to the effect of free solvent molecules on the reaction pathway of S at the cathode.

The greatly enhanced CE and prolonged cycle life of electrolytes with a high concentration of LiNO3 strongly suggest that Li2O is a beneficial SEI component, acting to prevent excessive decomposition of the electrolyte.
During repeated stripping and plating of Li metal, LiNO3 is consumed in a self-limiting manner as it passivates freshly exposed Li surfaces.
The small losses (inefficiencies) per cycle are a result of the consumption of LiNO3 during each plating/stripping cycle.
This is evidenced by the direct correlation of the practical cycle life of Li metal (i.e., high CE, > 98%) with the concentration of LiNO3 in the electrolyte.
When used as an additive (i.e., in small amounts), as is the case for the state-of-the-art DOL:DME electrolyte, the beneficial effect of LiNO3 in stabilizing the SEI is limited.
The SEI forms (and reforms) during each cycle, which relatively rapidly consumes all of the additive.
The use of LiTFSI as a co-salt is more critical to Li plating/stripping than the solvent selection.

This phenomena can be attributed to the more facile solvation and desolvation of Li+ cations in the presence of the TFSI- anion (e.g., its weaker coordination strength and reduced ionic association as compared to NO3 -) [27].
Only about 20% of the deposited Li is successfully stripped in the 1 M LiTFSI/G2 during each cycle and the remainder is built up as dead Li.
Dead Li is the direct result of a thick, insulating SEI which forms on the deposited Li surface leading to loss of contact with the current collector [31].
The increase in polarization is attributed to the build-up of an insulating layer on the two Li metal electrode surfaces [35].

Contrary to carbon, this reaction is self-limiting on Li metal surfaces, and Li is passivated by Li2O, which is why the nitrate is not rapidly consumed in the presence of Li metal anodes (as described above).

However, this simple experiment tells us that in Li-S batteries, the discharge cut-offvoltage must be set equal to or higher than 1.9 V or all of the nitrate in the electrolyte will be reduced at the carbon surface.
Comparisons of the S2p and N1s core level spectra (Fig.
S12) indicate that this is likely the result of less TFSI- decomposition in the presence of LiNO3.

While these anionic species are detected by XPS, we believe they play a minor role in the stabilization of Li metal relative to Li2O since these former species are very soluble in the electrolyte [37].
Based on the combination of NMR, FTIR, and XPS results here, we propose that Li2O is the key SEI component responsible for the improved performance of LiNO3-containing electrolytes in Li-S batteries.

This layer not only suppresses the reduction of the electrolyte co-salt, LiTFSI, and the solvent (G2 in the present study), it also clearly inhibits the reduction of soluble polysulfide species by the Li metal anode.

This, in turn, prevents the polysulfide shuttle mechanism and results in nearly a 100% CE for Li-S cells cycled with a catholyte (i.e., S active material dissolved in the electrolyte) and remarkable capacity retention.

The high concentration of LiNO3 serves two purposes: 1) to passivate the Li metal negative electrode, thus enabling > 99% CE for Li plating/stripping for an extended number of cycles, and 2) to increase the solubility of Li polysulfides (Li2Sn where 4 ≤n ≤8), thereby allowing the discharge/ charge process to occur via the liquid phase (electrolyte) rather than the reversible solid-state conversion of sulfur (S) to Li sulfide (Li2S).

The enhanced solubility of polysulfides in [0.5 M LiTFSI + 3 M LiNO3]/G2 relative to 1 M LiTFSI/ G2 is thought to be due to the higher ionic association strength of LiNO3 (than for LiTFSI) [27], similar to LiCF3SO3 in the work of Pan et al.
This outstanding performance using a catholyte is only possible with an electrolyte that allows Li metal plating/stripping to occur with exceptionally high CE. 4.

Although LiNO3 forms a very thin and stable SEI, preventing excessive decomposition of the G2 solvent and TFSI- anions, it forms during each deposition, remains after each stripping of the Li, and thus continuously builds up during cycling.

A highly mobile anion (due to its weaker interaction with Li+ cations) can lead to higher concentration of anions at Li−electrolyte interfaces resulting in enhanced salt decomposition and subsequent formation of a thick passivating SEI layer.

DMA has been reported to form dimethylamine in contact with lithium metal, suggesting particular instability with the central CN single bond.[31] Dimethylamine exists in the gas phase at room temperature, which may account for the relative decrease in intensity of the peak at 2.95 ppm, and the resultant byproducts may account for the preponderance of new peaks that appear (see Figure S6 , Supporting Information for more details).

MeIm solvent displays the largest degree of instability with lithium metal among all of the evaluated solvents, with the emergence of several new peaks as well as the absence of an expected peak at 7.6 ppm.

The complete absence of this peak clearly shows severe reaction with lithium metal has consumed the entire amount of MeIm reactant, and it suggests that the presence of the CN single bond may serve as a common point of lithium metal instability with DMA.

In the case of MeIm, a reaction occurring at this point could possibly open the imidazole ring, driving further side reactions and forming a multitude of decomposition products.[32] Further studies will likely be needed to confirm these hypotheses and have a more detailed understanding of the reactivity of these solvents with lithium metal.

Each of the attained spectra closely correlates to what is observed in baseline scans performed with pristine solvent, with no additional peaks occurring in the spectra besides known contaminants.[33] This signals that the applicability of the highly solvating electrolyte framework to polysulfide species is not intrinsically limited, and suggests that further improvements using this approach will likely have to focus on protecting the lithium–metal anode. 3.

At high sulfur loadings and low E/S ratios, increased solubility toward lithium polysulfide species can prolong the extent of solution-mediated discharge and enable the truly high specific energy promise of Li–S batteries.

DMSO and MeIm solvents exhibit diminished presence of S3•− at concentrated polysulfide conditions, which has a demonstrably negative effect on their ability to promote enhanced sulfur utilization compared to DMA solvent that displays substantial presence of S3•−.

Indeed, the ability to solvate a greater amount of polysulfide species and the preferential stabilization of S3•− are not completely dependent variables, though both seem to be bearers of increased solution-based utilization.

However, all of the high DN electrolytes exhibited inherent instability and uncontrolled decomposition in contact with lithium metal, as evident through investigations with electrochemical techniques and NMR.

On the other hand, a highly solvating electrolyte may yield great benefits to sulfur utilization at high areal sulfur loadings but would also present challenges to long-term cycling due to increased polysulfide shuttling.

Many approaches in the literature have demonstrated the opposite approach of impeding the dissolution of intermediate polysulfide species through sparingly soluble electrolytes.[15–17] Doing so can improve Li–S cyclability, as they minimize the shuttling and loss of active material over the course of cycling.
However, limiting solvation of polysulfide intermediates requires greater reliance on surface-dependent conduction pathways, which can be quite insulating and kinetically limiting in comparison.

KGaA, Weinheim 1803096 (7 of 9) on lithium–metal anode would be able to shield the undesirable reactions with these solvents, while additionally mitigating the loss of active material from the inevitable increased polysulfide shuttling in highly solvating electrolytes.

The clear blue color present in vials containing DMA and DMSO reveals the presence of the S3•− species.[5,22] This radical species is stabilized by the increased donicity of high DN solvents and can function as a redox mediator in solution.

Strong presence of the S3•− species at high concentration also does not seem to be directly correlated to either DN or dielectric constant, which may indicate the need for another metric in describing the preferential stabilization of radical species. 2.3.

Since solvent molecules are involved in the electrochemical reduction of sulfur and high-ordered lithium polysulfides, the depth of sulfur reduction is determined by the number of free solvent molecules, i.e., the solvent molecules not bound in solvate shells of lithium ions in the support salts.
It is further decreased at high concentrations of lithium perchlorate (above 2М) by the shortage of free solvent molecules required for the solvation of lithium polysulfides.

The subsequent decrease in the sulfur reduction depth in the descending region of the Qdisch. 1⁄4 f(Csalt) dependence can be explained by a considerable decline of the transport properties of the electrolyte system due to the increase in its viscosity (Fig. 6).

The increase in discharge voltage (Fig. 3) and the increase in the depth of electrochemical reduction of sulfur at the low voltage stage (Fig. 2), which observed in the ascending region of the Qdisch. 1⁄4 f(Csalt) dependence, indicate that the increase in lithium perchlorate concentration in the electrolyte solution results in the increase in the reactivity of sulfur into low-ordered lithium polysulfides (n  4).

The increase in Li2Sn reactivity is apparently due to an equilibrium shift of electrolytic dissociation of lithium polysulfides (Equations (1) and (2)) towards the formation of molecular species of lithium polysulfides that possess higher reactivity than ionic species.

The decrease in the discharge voltage at the high voltage stage with the increase in the support salt concentration (Fig. 3) is apparently due to the suppression of the homolytic dissociation of high-ordered lithium polysulfides.

The match of the positions of maxima on the concentration dependence of the capacity of lithium-sulfur cells and on the isotherm of lithium perchlorate solution conductivity indicates that the processes of ion transfer in the electrolyte solution and the depth of electrochemical reduction of sulfur are controlled by the same factors - the mobility and concentration of lithium ions.
We believe that the depth of the electrochemical reduction of lithium polysulfides is determined to a greater extent by the rate of charge transfer than by the transport properties of the medium.

The observed dependences of the resistance of lithium-sulfur cells at various depths of discharge on the concentration of lithium perchlorate confirm the hypothesis on the increase in the content of molecular species of lithium polysulfides with the increase in the concentration of support salts and the higher electrochemical activity of molecular species in comparison with ionic species. 4.6.

If this hypothesis is correct, the decrease in the rate of capacity depletion of lithium-sulfur cells during cycling with the increase in the support salt concentration can be explained by hindrance of sulfur and lithium sulfide crystallization in high-concentrated electrolyte solutions. 4.7.

The increase in the coulomb efficiency of cycling of lithiumsulfur cells with the increase in concentration of support salt is most likely due to the slowness of interelectrode sulfur transfer due to the increase in the viscosity of electrolyte solutions [50].

The decrease in the self-discharge (shuttle) current density of lithium-sulfur cells with the increase in the viscosity of solutions of lithium perchlorate in sulfolane (Fig. 5b) may indicate that the increase in the coulomb efficiency of cycling of lithium-sulfur cells with the increase in the concentration of the support salt is mainly due to the delay in interelectrode transfer of sulfur and lithium polysulfides. 5.

This is probably due to the fact that in high-concentrated electrolytes, because of their high viscosity, only a part of sulfur in the positive electrode is partly electrochemically reduced at the first cycles.

The decrease in coulomb efficiency at initial stages of cycling in electrolytes with low and moderate concentrations of lithium perchlorate can be due either to improvement of the transport properties of the surface film on the lithium electrode or to a growth of the lithium electrode surface due to dispersion of metallic lithium.

With subsequent cycling, the capacity of lithium-sulfur cells depletes mainly due to the simultaneous action of two factors - the decomposition of the electrolyte on the lithium electrode and the passivation of the surface of the carbon component of the sulfur electrode with poor soluble products of electrochemical reactions.
With a limited electrolyte content in lithium-sulfur cells after a certain number of cycles, the cell capacity decreases sharply to almost zero.

The solvation energy of the lithium ion in electrolyte systems with different concentrations of lithium perchlorate practically does not change, therefore discharge voltage is determined to a greater degree by the kinetics of the electrode processes than by the thermodynamics of solvation of the lithium ion.

Therefore, as the support salt concentration increases, the overall (diffusional and migrational) mobility of sulfur-containing particles decrease due to the increases in the viscosity of the electrolyte system.

We believe that the concentration of support salts affects the species of lithium polysulfides, their association-dissociation equilibria in electrolyte solutions and the processes of solvation of lithium ions contained in lithium polysulfides and support salts, and thus determines the performance of lithium-sulfur cells.

The lower solvation ability to the polysulfide could lower the utilization of sulfur,[21] thus the bare sulfur cathode–based Li/S batteries using TDE electrolyte shows relatively lower discharge capacity (≈200 mAh g−1 at 0.5 C) than LS002 electrolyte.
But it also brought some positive effects, the cycling stability of TDE electrolyte–based Li/S batteries is improved, the discharge capacity keeps almost unchanged over 900 cycles.
This could be attributed to the faster reaction kinetics of polysulfide with the help of CS separator.

Accelerated conversion of soluble high order polysulfide to insoluble low order polysulfide avoids the TDE electrolyte gets saturated, the continuous solvation ability of TDE electrolyte towards polysulfide improves the utilization of sulfur.
This is because higher amount of polysulfide dissolved into LS002 electrolyte and captured by nanoconductive carbon coating, thus the sulfur utilization is significantly improved in a short term.

Large amount of polysulfide dissolved out from cathode in cells using LS002 electrolyte, excess polysulfide can still pass through the nanoconductive carbon coating layer to reach the lithium metal anode, leading to the fast capacity fading.
The TDE electrolyte has a weaker ability to dissolve polysulfide, and the polysulfide shuttle is further inhibited with the help of the carbon coating layer on the cathode side of the separator.
What’s more, TDE electrolyte helps the lithium metal anode forming a dendritefree interface, thus the cells using TDE electrolyte is more stable than cells using LS002 electrolyte (Figure 7).

After several cycles of charge-discharge, the polysulfides dissolved into the electrolyte to form the “catholytes,” during the resting period of lithium–sulfur batteries, the as formed catholytes react with lithium metal anode spontaneously, causing self-discharge and resulting in voltage drop and irreversible capacity loss.[23] Due to the high solubility of LS002 electrolyte to the polysulfide, the severe shuttling effect can cause serious self-discharge, OCV of cells using conventional LS002 electrolyte shows an obvious decay from 2.35 to 2.15 V, which indicates severe capacity loss during resting (Figure S7, Supporting Information).
The released self-discharge in the Li–S cells can be ascribed to the reduced polysulfide solubility of TDE electrolyte.

Under the elevated temperature, conventional electrolytes are more reactive with lithium metal anode, continued consumption of electrolyte and severe shuttle of polysulfide cause a sharp capacity drop in high temperature.
TDE-CS separator–based batteries exhibit excellent stability and discharge capacity at 60 °C, which is due to optimized electrode-electrolyte interface.
TDE electrolyte and CS separator synergistically reduce polysulfides shuttling is also an important contributor.

The initial discharge capacity of Li/S batteries using LS002 electrolyte coupled with CS separator could reach up to 1223.9 mAh g−1, however, the deteriorated anode/electrolyte interface (Figure 6i) lead to low CE value (lowest CE value is at around 80.6%, the highest CE value is at around 93.8%) and rapid capacity decline.
First, the lower solubility to the polysulfides hinders the diffusion and shuttling effect, thereby ensuring higher capacity retention (83.6% capacity retention after 200 cycles at 0.5 C).

Second, rigid, flexible SEI film and dendrite free Li metal anode interface is formed during cycling, enables the stable cycling stability of Li/Li cells (cycled over 2500 hours with overpotential of less than 10 mV at current density of 1.0 mA cm−2 and 1.0 mAh cm−2) and Li-Cu cells, the electrolyte/electrode interface is stable enough even at 60 °C (870 mAh g−1 capacity remained after 100 cycles).

Both TDE and LS002 electrolyte steadily cycled over 2500 h at the current density of 1.0 mA cm−2 to a 1.0 mAh cm−2 capacity (Figure 3d), the overpotential of TDE electrolyte–based Li/Li symmetric cell is always less than the LS002 electrolyte–based Li/Li symmetric cell (insert plot in Figure 3d), which indicated the lower interface impedance of TDE electrolyte/electrode interface.

Conversely, the fluctuate CE value of Li/Cu cells with the LS002 electrolyte sharply declined during the charge/discharge process, such poor performance confirms the unstable reductive stability of LS002 electrolyte to Li metal anode.

Li metal electrode from Li/Li symmetric cells using the LS002 electrolyte shows a porous and fragmented surface (Figure 3e), the specific area of Li metal surface was enlarged thus more interfacial reactions would be introduced and causing unstable SEI interface and continuous electrolyte consumption.
The rough and easily peeled surface is easy to loss electrical connection with Li metal electrode and then bring about dead Li, which eventually leading to battery failure.

The huge surface energy of LiF makes it harder to get brittle fractured and the relatively smaller lattice constant allows easy plastic deformation,[18] the organic OCO component helps SEI more resilient, thus the soft and rigid LiF-rich SEI film generated by the TDE electrolyte decomposition can suppress the morphological instabilities, which is consistent well with SEM results.

The dendrite free character of TDE electrolyte greatly avoid the risks of internal short circuit thus the battery safety is further enhanced, the densely deposited Li layer helps mitigates the formation of dead Li, the long-term cycling stability of lithium metal anode is greatly improved.
The results of HOMO-LUMO calculation and XPS analysis prove that TTE can participates the SEI formation.
The voltage profiles change in the initial cycles can caused by the decomposing of tiny amount of LiNO3 in the TDE electrolyte.

During the initial several cycles, LiNO3 can be reduced to LiNxOy, Li2O species, and fast ion conductor such as Li3N and Li3N derivatives might be generated, thus the impedance of electrolyte/electrode surface can be decreased.

Herein, we report a new electrolyte formula for Li-S batteries under lean conditions, where 1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl 2,2,2- trifluoroethyl ether (TFTFE, Scheme 1) is employed as a cosolvent added to the electrolyte of 6 M lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (LiFSI) in DME.

In this study, we demonstrate that the TFTFE/DME/LiFSI electrolyte is highly compatible with LMA, where the average plating/stripping CE reaches 99.4% over 350 cycles, and the sulfur cathode delivers stable cycling performance under the lean-electrolyte conditions with E/S ratios of as low as 2.
Interestingly, we observed that more dilution by TFTFE in HE-5 does not benefit the cycling of the sulfur cathode, as shown in Figure S6.
This is a pioneering example of a full cell design, where an electrolyte facilitates excellent performance and reversibility of both electrodes under lean-electrolyte conditions.

This data support the hypothesis that NH4 + tends to associate more favorably with solvated polysulfide units than contiguous Li+ cations, disrupting the strong clustered Li+− Sx 2−frameworks that impede discharge behavior under kinetically limiting conditions.

For instance, this behavior may reflect the staged discharge of distinct mixed ammonium-lithium polysulfide species like what is seen in the NMR spectra of Figure 6b.

This shielding effect increases the relative softness of the cationic complex, which then proceeds to bind to the hard S2− discharge product less effectively.9,26 This in turn lowers the discharge potential of the second plateau, which can be interpreted as a change in the chemical activity of the constituent species from the Nernst equation.
Similarly, clustering of polysulfides increases the shielding of Li+, lowering the quasi-equilibrium potential of reduction.
The substitution of NH4 + serves to deter cluster formation, boosting the Li2S conversion potential as seen in the third plateau at 1.9 V.

However, NH4 + is a softer Lewis acid than Li+ and is more effectively solvated by surrounding DOL/DME molecules, which may drive the losses in potential seen in the second and fourth reduction plateaus.

This highly atypical and non-intuitive electrochemical behavior corroborates that the presence of NH4 + indeed transforms the coordination environment of dissolved polysulfide species away from the clustered lithium polysulfide aggregates typically seen under low-temperature conditions.

The divergence in the impact of this additive under the application of low temperatures and lean electrolyte amounts points to the driving influence of the polysulfide coordination environment on electrochemical performance.

Through a variety of electrochemical, spectroscopic, and computational studies, the in situ conversion of NH4TFA and lithium polysulfides to LiTFA and diammonium polysulfides is shown to amplify solution-mediated kinetics by deterring the formation of unfavorable clustered polysulfide aggregates.

This clustering behavior is found to be a relatively lower energy state and, as discussed, can occur disproportionately more frequently under lean electrolyte or low-temperature conditions.12−14 The selective coordination of lithium polysulfides to adjacent polysulfides in solution has been shown to be influenced and altered through the addition of strongly binding (high donor number) salt compounds like lithium trifluoroacetate (LiCO2CF3, abbreviated hereafter as LiTFA) to the electrolyte.13 The highly Lewis basic trifluoroacetate (TFA−) anion presents an effective electrostatic competing force to disrupt the strongly bound Li+−Sx 2−networks in favor of Li+− TFA−interactions, as illustrated in Figure 1b.

The mitigation of polysulfide clustering in turn has been shown to benefit kinetic behavior and capacity attainment under challenging lean electrolyte or low-temperature conditions.13,14 The anionic modification to the lithium polysulfide coordination environment presents an excellent platform to develop upon for further scientific insight and engineering improvement.

In summary, the findings of this work suggested the possible use of concentrated solutions based on end-capped glymes in efficient lithium−metal cells by careful tuning of (i) the ether chain length, (ii) the salt nature and concentration, (iii) the chemistry of the cathode material, and (iv) the operative conditions, including temperature and voltage limits.

This is because, in highconcentration electrolytes, almost all the solvent molecules are coordinated with salt cations, and there is almost no free solvent in the solution, which reduces the dissolution of the polysulfides.

In addition, in high-concentration electrolyte, Li salts are more likely to react with Li metal, forming a tremendously dense and robust solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer rich in inorganic components, which successfully prevent the corrosion of the Li metal.
Nevertheless, high-concentration electrolytes suffer from the hindrances of high viscidity, relatively low ionic conductivity, and expensive Li salts, which limit their commercial applications.

Meanwhile, more TFSIderived inorganic layers along with the organic outer layer arising from dimethoxyethane (DME) and dioxolane (DOL) solvent will build a robust SEI layer, which effectively improves the cyclic stability of the Li metal anode.
Consequently, increasing the concentration of the electrolyte can evidently enhance the reversibility of the Li metal, but still cannot build a stable Li anode for long cycling stability.

Since the reduction of free solvent in the solvated structure inhibited the dissolution of the polysulfides, the “shuttle effect” was suppressed.

The Li-deposition layer in LCE is relatively loose and unevenly distributed, and there are many small debris-like deposits among the Li deposition particles (Fig. 4a, b), which would destroy the cycling reversibility of the Li.

Secondly, for the practical optimization, the amount of HFE was able to be reduced due to the possible decomposition of HFE, but this caused an increase in viscosity and a decrease in wettability to the present cathode.

Therefore, under these low HFE conditions, the number of moles of LiTFSI to SL was reduced, thus increasing the free SL “to the extent that it does not dissolve the polysulfide” (examples are 2.0-, 1.5- and 1.0-SL), thereby increasing the activity of the cathode reaction.

Thus, a reduction in the Li-salt content of electrolytes could not only increase the reaction activity and reversibility but also reduce their cost and density, facilitating the practical applications of lithium-sulfur batteries.
Thus, while combining a microporous activated carbon-sulfur cathode with an SL-electrolyte system, the LiTFSI to SL ratio was a more important parameter than the viscosity and conductivity values.

The viscosity of the formulated electrolytes (0.5 to 2.5-SL) increased, and their conductivity decreased on increasing their lithium-salt content; this could be attributed to a decrease in the ion-transport rate due to high viscosity.

It is worth mentioning that high sulfur loading has also been recently achieved by replacing the conductive carbon matrix of the sulfur composite with metal or oxide particles,32,33 which is a consolidated strategy to achieve fast kinetics also employed in other devices as demonstrated in literature works.34−36 Additional strategies to improve the cathode performance may rely on optimized configurations including modified sulfurized polyacrylonitrile (SPAN)37 and multilayered structures exploiting synergic cathode chemistries.38,39 The already known high viscosity of TEGDME (3.3−3.7 mPa s)9,40 may represent a nonnegligible limit hindering the thin-layer cell application, particularly in view of the relatively low wettability of the laminated sulfur electrode using carbon-coated Al-support.41 This relevant issue can be mitigated by preparing binary solutions of TEGDME and a cosolvent with lower viscosity such as DOL (0.6 mPa s),42 hence allowing cell operation with limited charge-transfer resistance.43 Herein, we have proposed electrolytes predominantly including TEGDME with a limited fraction of DOL, i.e., either 5, 10, or 15 wt %.

The TGA (Figure 1a) and corresponding differential curves (DTG, Figure 1b) show for all electrolytes a first weight decrease at 150 °C with intensity growing alongside DOL concentration, likely due to the partial volatilization of the cyclic ether.53 The evaporation of TEGDME solvent takes place around 200 °C;53 however, the related weight loss is centered at 197 °C for TE-5%, 210 °C for TE-10%, and 263 °C for TE-15%.

Furthermore, the combination of TEGDME and DOL is expected to reciprocally compensate the respective drawback of the two solvents, that is, the high viscosity of the former and the relevant flammability and low stability toward the Li2Sx intermediates of the latter.

The TE-10% appears to be the most promising compromise since the corresponding Li−S cell shows the longer cycle life likely ascribed to the optimal proportion between TEGDME and DOL, despite the fluctuation of the capacity during cycling, which may be assessed by improving the cathode configuration.

The above results indicate that a suitable electrolyte for lithium−metal anodes and Cmicro−meso−S cathodes requires a low viscosity and high LiFSI concentration.

Diluted electrolytes with HFE have reduced viscosity and localized high concentrations of LiFSI because LiFSI does not dissolve in HFE.24 Herein, 3 M LiFSI/ DME was diluted with HFE to improve the cycling performance at high current densities and suppress Li2Sx dissolution.

As a result, the Li−S batteries exhibited high discharge capacity (830 mA h g−1 at the 50th cycle), high average coulombic efficiency (98.5%), and high-rate performance because the following factors were achieved simultaneously: • The suppression of Li2Sx dissolution by reducing the amount of uncoordinated DME due to HFE dilution; • The reduction of the viscosity of the electrolyte due to HFE dilution; • The densification of deposited Li caused by increasing the local concentration of the electrolyte; and • The formation of a thin SEI on the anode because the decomposition of FSI−is suppressed due to the appropriate DME/HFE ratio.

If the HFE ratio is high in the electrolyte, that is, the local concentration is high, FSI−coordinated to Li+ increases, resulting in the formation of an LiF-rich SEI due to the decomposition of FSI−.

The electrolyte used in this study contains a high percentage of DME, which prevents significant anionic decomposition.57 ■CONCLUSIONS In this study, we investigated porous carbon as a sulfur host and the electrolyte composition suitable for Li−S batteries with high-concentration LiFSI/DME.

As a result, the Li−S batteries exhibited high discharge capacity (830 mA h g−1 at the 50th cycle), high average coulombic efficiency (98.5%), and high-rate performance because the following factors were achieved simultaneously: • The suppression of Li2Sx dissolution by reducing the amount of uncoordinated DME due to HFE dilution; • The reduction of the viscosity of the electrolyte due to HFE dilution; • The densification of deposited Li caused by increasing the local concentration of the electrolyte; and • The formation of a thin SEI on the anode because the decomposition of FSI−is suppressed due to the appropriate DME/HFE ratio.

The capacity decay of the Cmicro−meso−S/ Li battery with 3 M LiFSI/DME was due to Li2Sx dissolution caused by a few mesopores and uncoordinated DME molecules.

Some reports have shown that high-concentration electrolytes contain less uncoordinated DME; thus, the Li2Sx dissolution is suppressed.24,45 High-concentration LiFSI/DME above 3.6 M without uncoordinated DME would realize Cmicro−meso−S/Li batteries with high energy density and high cycle stability.

In the case of 3.6 and 4 M LiFSI/DME, nearly all of the DME were coordinated to Li+ because the molar ratios of LiFSI and DME were 1:2 and 1:1.4, respectively.22 Thus, the dissolution of Li2Sx was significantly inhibited and the highpotential plateau disappeared.
A highly concentrated electrolyte has a high viscosity and low ionic conductivity (Table 2), which leads to a non-uniform Figure 4.
current distribution at the cathode.
This phenomenon at the cathode also induces a non-uniform current distribution at the anode, resulting in a lower coulombic efficiency.

In contrast, at a very low current density (0.02 C), the coulombic efficiency of the Li−S batteries improved with increasing electrolyte concentration because the non-uniform current distribution was mitigated (Figure 4c).

Thus, the high-concentration LiFSI/DME electrolyte effectively improved the Li deposition morphology and suppressed Li2Sx dissolution; however, its high viscosity reduced the Li−S battery performance at high current densities.
Dilution with HFE increased the concentration of LiFSI in DME, which decreased the amount of free DME.
Therefore, the dissolution of Li2Sx was suppressed in 3 M LiFSI in DME/HFE.

Higher-concentration electrolytes have fewer free solvent molecules; thus, the Li2S8 added to higher-concentration electrolytes does not exist stably and is thought to be transformed to shorter-chain Li2Sx.
This improved cycling performance with HFE dilution was due to the mitigation of the non-uniform current distribution by decreasing the viscosity of the electrolyte (Table 2).

Furthermore, the surface of Li in 3 M LiFSI in DME/HFE had more Li0 than that in 3 M LiFSI/ DME at a sputtering time of 2.4−23 min.53,54 Therefore, the depth profile suggests that the SEI on Li in 3 M LiFSI in DME/HFE is thinner than that in 3 M LiFSI/DME because of the suppression of FSI−decomposition on the Li anode by HFE dilution.

However, it has been reported that HFE dilution of high-concentration LiFSI/DME facilitates the decomposition of FSI−; thus, LiF is enriched.55,56 Our results contradict those of previous studies because the amount of HFE in the electrolyte was lower than that reported in previous studies.

If the HFE ratio is high in the electrolyte, that is, the local concentration is high, FSI−coordinated to Li+ increases, resulting in the formation of an LiF-rich SEI due to the decomposition of FSI−.

The electrolyte used in this study contains a high percentage of DME, which prevents significant anionic decomposition.57 ■CONCLUSIONS In this study, we investigated porous carbon as a sulfur host and the electrolyte composition suitable for Li−S batteries with high-concentration LiFSI/DME.

As a result, the Li−S batteries exhibited high discharge capacity (830 mA h g−1 at the 50th cycle), high average coulombic efficiency (98.5%), and high-rate performance because the following factors were achieved simultaneously: • The suppression of Li2Sx dissolution by reducing the amount of uncoordinated DME due to HFE dilution; • The reduction of the viscosity of the electrolyte due to HFE dilution; • The densification of deposited Li caused by increasing the local concentration of the electrolyte; and • The formation of a thin SEI on the anode because the decomposition of FSI−is suppressed due to the appropriate DME/HFE ratio.

Because HFE is one of the hydrofluoroethers with the lowest lithium-solvating ability,28 dilution with HFE significantly reduces the viscosity of high-concentration LiFSI/ DME while maintaining the locally high concentration of the LiFSI/DME electrolyte.29 Moreover, HFE suppresses the side reaction between Li2Sx and lithium−metal anodes, and improves the deposition morphology of lithium−metal anodes;30 thus, HFE is a promising solvent for electrolyte optimization.

Herein, hexyl methyl ether (HME) is proposed as an outer shell solvent to construct HME-based EPSE (HME- EPSE) to balance the rate and cycle performance of practical Li� S batteries.

Results and Discussion Solvation structure of LiPSs in HME-EPSE The weak solvating power and high reduction stability toward Li metal are two basic conditions of the outer solvent in EPSE to regulate the solvation structure of LiPSs.
Therefore, HME meets the two basic conditions to construct EPSE and thus is used to formulate HME-EPSE (DOL/DME/HME= 37.5/37.5/25, by vol.).

Conclusion In conclusion, HME is proposed as a co-solvent to formulate EPSE so that the rate performance of S cathodes and the protection of Li metal anodes are balanced in Li� S batteries under practical conditions (Figure 5).

This work reveals the potential of modulating the solvation structure of LiPSs in EPSE to regulate the reaction kinetics at both anode and cathode sides and to achieve the balanced performance of Li� S batteries.

Introduction Electrification emerges as a promising strategy for decarburization in the pursuit of net-zero emissions.[1] The development of high-energy-density application areas, such as longendurance unmanned aerial vehicles, urgently requires advanced high-energy-density rechargeable batteries.[2] Lithium� sulfur (Li� S) battery with an ultrahigh theoretical energy density of 2600 Whkg� 1 is regarded as a promising next-generation battery candidate.[3] Li� S batteries with energy density over 500 Whkg� 1 at the cell level have been realized.[3d] However, the practical applications of Li� S batteries are still plagued by their poor cycle life under demanding conditions including a high-loading S cathode (> 6.0 mgScm� 2), a low electrolyte/sulfur (E/S) ratio (< 3.0 μLmgS � 1), and a limited Li metal inventory (<100 μm).[4] The short cycle life of Li� S batteries mainly results from the rapid depletion of lean electrolytes and limited active Li.[4a,5] Concretely, massive soluble Li polysulfides (LiPSs) are generated in the S cathode to enable typical solid� liquid� solid conversion reactions and provide high discharge-specific-capacity over 1000 mAhg� 1 due to rapid charge transfer and redox mediation.[6] However, LiPSs can diffuse to the anode side through a concentration gradient and induce severe parasitic reactions with Li metal anodes, which further results in the notorious shuttle effect.[7] The parasitic reactions deplete active Li inventory, active LiPSs, and electrolytes, finally leading to rapid battery failure.[8] Under mild conditions with an excessive Li inventory (thickness>500 μm), flooded electrolytes (E/S ratio> 15 μLmgS � 1), and a low-loading S cathode (<2.0 mgScm� 2), Li� S batteries can generally deliver stable cycle performance owing to much excessive Li inventory despite the existence of the parasitic reactions.[9] However, under demanding conditions as mentioned above, meager active materials are rapidly depleted, severely shortening the cycle life of practical Li� S batteries.[10] The solvation structure of LiPSs plays a vital role in dictating the reaction kinetics with Li metal anodes as reported.[11] Therefore, regulating the solvation structure of LiPSs emerges as a promising strategy to improve the cycle performance of Li� S batteries.

Encapsulating Li-polysulfide electrolyte (EPSE) was proposed to inhibit the parasitic reactions between LiPSs and Li metal anodes, where LiPSs are encapsulated by a bilayer solvation shell.[12] With strong-solvating-power solvents in the inner layer, such as 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME), the solid� liquid� solid conversion reactions of S cathode are allowed.[13] The outer shell solvents with weak [*] L.-L.

solvating power and superior reduction stability to Li metal impair the reactivity of LiPSs with Li metal anodes kinetically, such as di-isopropyl sulfide (DIPS), isopropyl ether (DIPE), and 1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl-2,2,3,3-tetrafluoropropyl ether (HFE).[12,14] Although available EPSEs attempt to maintain smooth conversion reactions of S cathode furthest, adverse effects are inevitable for S conversion reaction kinetics, especially at high working rat es.[12,14–15] Specifically, the specific capacity of S cathodes in current EPSEs decreases by over 50 mAhg� 1, and the polarization at the second discharge plateau increases by 0.05–0.2 V at working rates around 0.1 C.

The cause of this surprising result is unclear, but we suspect that the use of a lower Li ion concentration increased the concentration of dissolved polysulfide, which might have caused an increase in the viscosity.

The ability of the low Li ion concentration cell to avoid a continued voltage drop is an indication that there must exist some mechanism for the cell to manage and regulate the high concentration of polysulfide.

This is somewhat unexpected given its known dependence on the polysulfide concentration43 and suggests that a high viscosity of the electrolyte stemming from polysulfide dissolution might not be a great sole predictor of performance.
Cells with a higher Rint‐P2/Rint‐P1 performed better, indicating that the precipitation of these solid-sulfur species likely help to alleviate the high concentration of the cell discharged under LEC.

Consequently, cells that do not have a high Rint,P2 (when normalized to Rint,P1) are unable to form such redissolvable species (i.e., RPSS) and unable to eliminate/avoid the sources (clustering/aggregates/gelation) of chronic overpotentials.
One possible explanation is that the more stable the clusters, the higher the degree of supersaturation and the poorer its ability to precipitate out as an RPSS.

polysulfide species, which only appear at low Li ion concentrations, supporting the notion that higher Li ion concentrations stabilize polysulfide solution against precipitation.

A corollary of such a finding is that a stronger interaction between solvent and lithium polysulfide and lithium salts could provide an unwanted stabilizing effect of polysulfide clusters in solution during discharge.

This is likely detrimental to LEC LSB, which is in contrast to the common notion of increasing the solubility limit of polysulfide by using more polar solvents.23,46 Stronger solvating solvents will tend to interact more strongly with polysulfide and Li ions.

However, in flooded cells, where the concentration regime of polysulfide is much lower, notable performance enhancements have indeed been previously reported.47 From our results, the problem of lean E/S ratio (high concentration of polysulfide) does not depend on merely the solubility but is more related to the existing concentration of polysulfide in the electrolyte and the proclivity of aggregation/ clustering.
Such clustering of polysulfide limits the formation of RPSSs and the polysulfide concentration cannot be regulated or remedied over the course of discharge.

Poorly dissociated Li salts could disrupt the formation of these lithium polysulfide clusters, as a significant portion of Li ions are already paired with their original anion and cannot participate in cluster formation.

It was proposed that a decrease in Li ion concentration will benefit the performance, citing an increased discharge capacity when using an E/S ratio of 3.5 μL mgs −1.49 At a very lean E/S ratio of <3.0 μL mgs −1, we observe that lowering Li ion concentration still exhibits a large overpotential.
The second peak was not observed likely to the poor kinetics of the reduction process under Li ion-rich conditions, which corroborates nicely with the galvanostatic discharge (Figure 2a).

However, when the Li ion content was reduced to 0.05 M LiTFSI and 0.025 M LiNO3, we begin to observe two distinct peaks (∼2.25 and ∼1.95 V), indicating a better ability of the cell to reduce sulfur polysulfide and also to reduce polysulfides to Li2S/Li2S2.
We attribute this to the ability to form more RPSS as the lack of free Li ions limits the formation of stabilized polysulfide aggregates.
The increase in diffusion coefficient from LiTF addition aligns with the notion that polysulfide clustering/aggregates has been disturbed.
This suggests that the large increase in Li diffusion is unable to increase the discharge voltage up to >2.0 V.

Since only a marginal increase in Li diffusion coefficient with LiTF addition was observed for the 5 M polysulfide sample, we suspect that the main benefit of LiTF is not in enhancing Li transport but in promoting the formation of RPSS.
Finally, we note that the use of low Li ion concentration electrolytes might lead to problems such as the lowered Li ion conductivity in the electrolyte.
Furthermore, use of low amounts of LiNO3 is likely to hinder cyclability as the Li metal will be less passivated against polysulfide shuttling.

Conclusion In this work, we demonstrated that LiFPB served as a highly effective co-salt for Li-S batteries by simultaneously addressing two critical challenges: the polysulfide shuttle effect and the Li metal anode degradation.

Mechanistically, the incorporation of LiFPB facilitated the formation of a robust SEI layer enriched with LiF and LiBxOy components, which significantly suppressed electrolyte decomposition and enabled homogeneous Li plating/stripping.
Cyclic voltammetry (CV) tests demonstrated that, when conventional electrolytes are employed, the lithium-sulfur battery displays reduced redox peak currents across varying scan rates.

This observation indicates that the transport of ions and electrons within the battery is hindered during the charge and discharge cycles, thereby impeding the overall electrochemical performance of the battery.
Spectroscopic and electrochemical analyses revealed that LiFPB facilitate the formation of lithium borate (LiBxOy) complexes at the lithium metal interface.
These boratecontaining species serve as rapid lithium-ion conductors within the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI),[24–27] facilitating the uniform deposition of Li metal (Figure 3f).

By combining ab-initio molecular dynamics simulations, spectral characterization, and insitu measurements of the electrochemical cell, it is confirmed that the stereochemistry manipulation endows the electrolyte with a weakened solvation ability to enhance the reaction kinetics and forms an encapsulated polysulfide solvation structure to prohibit the anode parasitic reactions from polysulfides.

Meanwhile, the shrinkage in molecular volume would endow MPE with less steric effect to accelerate Li+ de-solvation process and block the Li+-ether complex, thus increasing the reaction kinetics [32].
The viscosity simulation results and experimental test results jointly validate that the MPE-incorporated electrolyte exhibits ultra-low viscosity (Fig.
S2), which facilitates the ionic mass transfer within electrolyte, thus enhancing the overall effi­ ciency of the electrochemical processes involved in Li-S cells.

Theoretically, better wettability of the electrolyte on the material’s surface leads to improved interfacial kinetics and less electrolyte required to maintain the same reaction kinetics, which is advantageous for achieving better electrochemical performance under lean electrolyte condition, thus increasing the energy density of cell [38].
More interestingly, we found the lowest unoccupied molecular orbit (LUMO) energy level of MPE is elevated distinctly (Fig.
S4), which insinuates the improved reduction stability and better compatibility with both the PS species and Li anode [41,42], according to the frontier orbital theory.

This is also substantially vali­ dated by the reduction stability tests, where the MPE-incorporated saltfree electrolyte shows an ameliorated side reaction currents comparing with its counterpart (Fig. 1d).

These Raman results confirm the fact that the solvent activity of DME solvent is substantially decreased by the addition of the weakly solvating MPE, meanwhile LiNO3 and LiTFSI would be preferentially reduced on the lithium sur­ face, which is underpinned by the 7Li nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) measurements.

Hence, the MPE molecules tend to distribute in the outer solvent shell around PS and the inner shell is mainly composed of DOL and DME [28], by which PS are encapsulated in anti-reductive solvent shells to decrease its reactivity towards Li anode, as schematically illustrated in Fig. 2f.

The above results indicate that the incorporation of MPE could optimize the electrolyte structure, in which the MPE molecules serve as the building blocks of the outer solvent shell where the parasitic reactions between the PS and Li metal are kinetically obstructed by the anti-reductive shell, thus promoting the kinetics of electrode reaction and mitigating its exposure to fresh Li.

The FES simulation results strongly prove that the decrease in carbonchain length induces a reduced steric hindrance for the accessibility of Li+ to the PS monomer, which accelerates the sulfur transformation during SRR process.

Therefore, STE furnishes a more stable cell oper­ ation environment, minimizing the decomposition of the electrolyte and the formation of deposits.

These effects should not only suppress its capability to dissolve poly­ sulfides but also facilitate the formation of a LiF-rich SEI layer on the surface of the anode along with homogeneous Li deposition.

CID spectra revealed that Li+ exhibits preferential solvation in different fluoropyridines, with 2FPy showing a stronger interaction with Li+ than 4FPy and 3FPy, likely due to the ortho-fluorine interaction unique to 2FPy.
According to calculations by Choi et al.,25 the DNs for 2FPy and 3FPy are 15.8 and 29.7 kcal mol−1, respectively, suggesting that 3FPy should exhibit a stronger interaction with Li+ than 2FPy.

However, this prediction is inconsistent with the CID data (Table 1), which shows that a relative abundance of [2FPy + Li]+ is 55.1% (compared to the abundance of [Py + Li]+) and the relative abundance of [3FPy + Li]+ is only 9.6%.
Moreover, based on the calculated DNs of 2-, 3-, and 4-fluoropyridine (2FPy, 3FPy, and 4FPy), they attributed the high solubility of polysulfide in 3FPy with its high DN.25 2.

Through solvation tests and XPS analysis, they found that the high solubility of polysulfides and the high LiF content in the SEI layer were key factors contributing to the excellent cyclability of the Li−S battery with very high sulfur loading, even under LiNO3-free and lean electrolyte conditions.

Interestingly, a comparison of HPLC results, as listed in Tables S-2 and S-4, reveals that the addition of the LiTFSi salt reduces the polysulfide solubility in 2FPy and 3FPy, whereas it unexpectedly increases the polysulfide solubility in Py and DME/DOL.

The underlying cause of this phenomenon remains unclear, underscoring the complexity of the solvation process and highlighting the limitation of using the solvent donor number alone to interpret the solvation behavior.

Specifically, the discharge profile of the Li−S battery with the 3FPy electrolyte showed an extended high discharge plateau (corresponding to the reduction of elemental sulfur to long-chain polysulfides) and a reduced low discharge plateau (representing the reduction of long-chain to short-chain polysulfides and sulfides) relative to the 2FPy electrolyte.

Additionally, a second charge plateau appears around 2.4 V in the charge profile for the 3FPy electrolyte, a feature characteristic of Li−S batteries cycling in electron pair donor (EPD) electrolytes, such as N-dimethylacetamide (DMA) or dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO).

For example, in DMSO electrolytes, the second discharge plateau appeared below 2 V due to the stabilization of S3 −radicals by the EPD solvent.30 Choi et al. also confirmed the existence of S3 −radicals in the Py electrolyte and in the 3FPy electrolyte by UV−vis spectrometry.25 Negative electrospray ionization mass spectrometry ((−)ESI/MS) was employed to investigate lithium polysulfide Figure 2.

Additionally, in the charge/discharge profile of the Li−S battery with the 2FPy electrolyte (Figure 2C), a small but clear discharge plateau appears between 2.4 and 2.6 V after extended cycling, although it is absent at the beginning and only emerges gradually with cycling.

According to the prior research on organodisulfides (e.g., dipyridyl disulfides) by Fu et al.,32 this small discharge plateau above 2.4 V likely results from organosulfide species formed through the ongoing reactions between 2FPy and polysulfides during the cycling.

In contrast, due to the different reactivity of 3FPy and the electron-withdrawing effect of meta-fluorine, 3FPy remains stable without reacting with polysulfides, as demonstrated in Figures 2E, 3A, and 4A.
Remarkably, the addition of LiNO3 to the 3FPy electrolyte significantly reduced the shuttle effect, although the capacity retention remained suboptimal (Figure S-18D).
For the 2FPy electrolyte, the low solubility of LiNO3 limited its stabilizing effect, and even with saturation of LiNO3, the Li−S battery with 2FPy overcharged severely at 60 °C (Figure S-18B).
These findings underscore the crucial role of LiNO3 in stabilizing the SEI layer on the Li anode, even in fluoropyridine-based electrolytes.

It should be noted that the solubility of Li2Sx in the electrolyte with 1.0 M LiTFSI is higher than that with 0.8 M LiTFSI, possibly because more Li+ in 1.0 M LiTFSI increases the formation of Li3S6 + positive ions or polarized ether molecules, promoting the amount of dissolved Li2Sx species.

In short, due to the insulation property of S/Li2S, the conventional solid−liquid−solid reaction path with limited long-range electron transfer occurs in the electrolyte with a limited amount of unpolarized ether (1 M LiTFSI, Figure 2j).

In stark contrast, due to the improved S8 solubility in the electrolyte with an increased amount of unpolarized ether (0.8 M LiTFSI), the liquid−liquid−solid reaction pathway with an enhanced long-range electron transfer route is constructed.
This suggests that the reduction reaction rate is low and S is not completely reduced.
Moreover, Li2Sx peaks completely disappear at 1.91 V, indicating complete S reduction due to a greatly increased reaction rate (Figure 3c).

Studies have shown that lowering the lithium salt concentration can induce the Li2S deposition mode from transient nucleation to continuous nucleation.19 These results demonstrate that an increase of S8 solubility in the electrolyte by increasing the amount of unpolarized ether molecules converts the original solid−liquid−solid into the liquid−liquid−solid reaction pathway for better S8 utilization.

A comparison between the spectra of 0.2Se and 0.2Se-N reveals a red shift in the characteristic Se-Se peaks located at 213 and 313 cm− 1 .
This shift indicates that the highly electronegative Se atoms in DPDSe preferentially coordinate with Li+ ions.
This coordination causes the electron cloud of the Se-Se bond to shift toward the Li+ ion, weakening the bond strength and facilitating the formation of contact ion pairs (CIP) [ 35 ].
In contrast, a comparison between 0.2Te and 0.2Te- N shows a blue shift in the C-Te-Te characteristic band at 172 cm− 1 .

By integrating a single -CF3 group exclusively at the terminal of the highly flexible DME back­ bone, C14 strategically balances three critical requirements within a single molecule: (1) sufficient solvating power to dissolve 1.0 M LiTFSI, (2) the delocalization of molecular surface charge to suppress poly­ sulfide ionization, and (3) a practically viable boiling point of 104 ◦C, which enables stable vacuum filling procedures.

Therefore, the C14-based electrolyte provides a promising conceptual pathway toward achieving high-energy-density Li-S batteries by combining a relatively low-density profile with the inherent capability to suppress polysulfide leaching without relying on excessively high salt concentrations.
This work establishes that suppressing solvent-induced ionization via charge delocalization is a vital strategy for realizing stable, high-performance Li-S batteries. 1.

More broadly, this work highlights that molecular design focusing on charge delocalization in fluorinated ethers serves as a highly effective and generalizable strategy for developing advanced electro­ lytes in next-generation Li-S batteries.

Conclusions HFE is used as a superior outer-shell solvent to construct EPSE to inhibit the intrinsic side reactions between LiPSs and Li-metal anodes.

According to previous advances, large steric hindrance can effectively weaken the solvating power of molecules[17] and the isopropyl with large steric hindrance makes di-isopropyl sulfide (DIPS) and isopropyl ether (DIPE) to act as effective outer-shell solvents to construct EPSE.[16] However, there is difference in the solvating power between DIPS and DIPE due to the different coordination atoms (S atom in DIPS and O atom in DIPE) and they display different improvement effects on the cycle lifespan of Li–S batteries.[16] Therefore, it is speculated that the solvating power of outer-shell solvents plays a vital role in dictating the effect of EPSE and the underlying mechanism is indistinct.

Compared with previous research that the introduction of DIPS and DIPE has a little influence of deshielding effect on the chemical shift of 7Li, the decoded solvation structure of HFE-EPSE indicates that the solvating power of HFE is much weaker than DIPS and DIPE, which is beneficial from the large steric hindrance of fluorohydrocarbon chains and electron-withdrawing effect of CF2 segments.
There are two long fluorohydrocarbon chains with large steric hindrance and abundant electronwithdrawing CF2 segments in the HFE molecule, which enables HFE to have much weak solvating power.
This work demonstrates that HFE is a superior outer-shell solvent to construct EPSE and inspires further effective regulation of solvation structures of LiPSs to achieve long-cycling Li–S batteries.

In this work, through adopting the sparingly solvated electrolyte DME1.6LiFSI-HFE with a low DN of 13.9, the dissolution of polysulfides was suppressed to an extremely low level.

From the reduction potential in different electrolytes, we estimate the upper limit of reduction potential that enables the Li-S battery to work under a lean-electrolyte condition lies in the range of 2.16−2.19 V.
Once the reduction potential exceeds this limit, the solvation capability of the electrolyte is too high and is incapable of suppressing polysulfide dissolution effectively.

We have to admit that it is a great challenge to avoid the electrolyte consumption in the lithium−metal anode at such a high area capacity (10 mAh cm−2) and high current density without extra protection of the lithium−metal anode.

However, we still have the confidence that the electrolyte consumption can be alleviated either by electrolyte optimization or lithium anode protection in the near future, so as to enable a high practical energy density Li-S battery to work stably for dozens of cycles (e.g., 50 cycles ending up with 500 Wh kg−1). ■CONCLUSIONS In conclusion, we found that the real solubility of sulfide in the electrolyte is far more than the 6−7 MS reported in the literature by using an evaporation method to test the solubility, which could influence the viscosity of the electrolyte and eventually cause a gelation transition (where E/S is reduced to a certain extent by the liquid into a solid electrolyte), affecting the utilization efficiency of active substances and PGED of the Li-sulfur battery.

However, highly soluble LiPSs in the conventional 1,3-­dioxolane/1,2-­ dimethoxyethane (DOL/DME) electrolyte (solubility, ~1,100 mM based on S atom, [S]) (10) diffuse to the anode side and react with Li metal (i.e., notorious LiPS shuttling effect), causing rapid capacity fade, low Coulombic efficiency (CE) (11), and severe self-­discharge (12–14).
However, electrolytes with ultrahigh and high solubility of LiPSs suffered from significant shuttling effect and instability against Li metal anode (10, 26).

Although decreasing the LiPS solubility has been shown to be effective in reducing capacity decay from the shuttling effect, low concentration of polysulfides would sacrifice the Li-­S conversion kinetics to release full capacity during cycling (35).

The solubility of LiPSs in most previously reported sparingly solvating electrolytes was lower than 50 mM [S], leading to sluggish Li-­S conversion (requiring elevated operation temperature, ≥55 °C) and low S capacity utilization (24, 28, 32, 36).
For electrolytes with ultrahigh/high solubility of LiPSs, such as DMI and DOL/DME, the shuttling effect limits the cell performance (fast capacity decay and low CE) (37).

On the contrary, the cell performance using electrolytes with low/ultralow LiPS solubilities is limited by the sluggish Li-­S reaction (low capacity utilization and short cycle life) due to the high electron/ ion transfer resistance in the solid-­solid S-­Li2S electrochemistry (35) (SI Appendix, Fig.
The solubility of LiPSs is related to the solvation ability of Li+ in the electrolytes (38).

In conventional ether electrolytes (e.g., DME), Li+ ions are solvated by DME to form a stable five-­member ring structure (Li+ clamped by two –O– groups) (39), which enhances the cation–anion separation of LiPSs and thus results in high solubility of LiPSs.

We identified that the SCN−-coordinated Li+ solvation structure facilitates the formation of the Li3N-rich SEI layer, which improves the reversibility of the Li metal electrode.

For the LiSCN electrolyte, a C=N peak at 399.25 eV was examined and the intensity of the Li3N peak was much higher than the other electrolytes, which suggests the participation of SCN−in the SEI formation.[37] This result also presents a scenario in which the highly conductive Li3N-enriched SEI layer is responsible for the enhanced cycling stability observed for the LiSCN electrolyte.

The C-S peak was found only for the SCN electrolyte, which supports the involvement of SCN− in the SEI formation.[39] The impedance, SEM, and XPS analysis collectively indicate that SCN−actively contributes to SEI formation, and the resulting SEI layer enables uniform Li deposition, thus diminishing solvent decomposition.
