Notably, the solvation structure derived from medium solvating power electrolyte balances the cathode and anode kinetics and therefore improves the cycling performance of working Li� S batteries.

On one hand, LiPSs act as important intermediates of the solid–liquid– solid conversion reactions and are involved in every electrochemical process at the cathode.[4a] Fast cathode kinetics of LiPSs promises rapid electrochemical conversion and full utilization of the active materials,[7] thus realizing high specific capacity and maintaining high capacity retention.[8] Conversely, sluggish cathode kinetics induces aggravated polarization to result in rapid capacity loss and quick failure of Li� S batteries.[9] On the other hand, the dissolved LiPSs are highly reactive and can chemically react with Li metal once diffused to the anode side.[10] Fast anode kinetics of LiPSs induces severe parasitic reactions on Li metal anodes and rapid depletion of limited Li reservoir.[11] Furthermore, the by-products between LiPSs and Li metal participate in the formation of solid electrolyte interphase (SEI), further deteriorating the transport uniformity of Li ions and exacerbating inhomogeneous Li deposition.[12] Accordingly, fast anode kinetics of LiPSs results in rapid decay of Li metal anodes and limited cycling lifespan of Li� S batteries.[13] Considering the consistent variation of the cathode and anode kinetics, the effects of LiPS electrode kinetics at the cathode and anode on the cycling performance of Li� S batteries are intrinsically contradictory.[14] Therefore, it is extremely necessary to reasonably regulate the LiPS electrode kinetics, specifically, reducing the LiPS anode kinetics without severely deteriorating the LiPS cathode kinetics to construct practical long-cycling Li� S batteries.

Moreover, the Li� S coin cell with the mid-weak solvation structure delivers an ultra-long cycling lifespan of 146 cycles with an initial specific capacity of 887 mAhg� 1 and a capacity retention of 78.5% due to the balanced cathode and anode kinetics.

The Li� S pouch cell with the medium solvation structure delivers a prolonged cycling lifespan of 30 cycles with an initial energy density of 338 Whkg� 1 based on the total mass of the whole pouch cell (Table S4).
Consequently, only the Li� S pouch cell with the medium solvation structure possesses moderate electrode kinetics of both the cathode and the anode and thus achieves a prolonged cycling lifespan.

Balancing the cathode and anode kinetics through regulating the solvating power of the LiPS solvation structure is validated to be effective in realizing high-energy-density and long-cycling Li� S pouch cells.

On one hand, LiPSs act as important intermediates of the solid–liquid– solid conversion reactions and are involved in every electrochemical process at the cathode.[4a] Fast cathode kinetics of LiPSs promises rapid electrochemical conversion and full utilization of the active materials,[7] thus realizing high specific capacity and maintaining high capacity retention.[8] Conversely, sluggish cathode kinetics induces aggravated polarization to result in rapid capacity loss and quick failure of Li� S batteries.[9] On the other hand, the dissolved LiPSs are highly reactive and can chemically react with Li metal once diffused to the anode side.[10] Fast anode kinetics of LiPSs induces severe parasitic reactions on Li metal anodes and rapid depletion of limited Li reservoir.[11] Furthermore, the by-products between LiPSs and Li metal participate in the formation of solid electrolyte interphase (SEI), further deteriorating the transport uniformity of Li ions and exacerbating inhomogeneous Li deposition.[12] Accordingly, fast anode kinetics of LiPSs results in rapid decay of Li metal anodes and limited cycling lifespan of Li� S batteries.[13] Considering the consistent variation of the cathode and anode kinetics, the effects of LiPS electrode kinetics at the cathode and anode on the cycling performance of Li� S batteries are intrinsically contradictory.[14] Therefore, it is extremely necessary to reasonably regulate the LiPS electrode kinetics, specifically, reducing the LiPS anode kinetics without severely deteriorating the LiPS cathode kinetics to construct practical long-cycling Li� S batteries.

Employing weakly-solvating electrolyte effectively prolongs the cycling lifespan via suppressing the anode corrosion but inevitably results in severe cathode capacity degradation under lean-electrolyte conditions.
However, the dissolved LiPSs chemically react with lithium metal and inevitably corrode the lithium anode continuously, which is widely acknowledged to cause the shuttle effect [20–22].

The corrosion of lithium anode by the dissolved LiPSs irreversibly consumes the limited active lithium reservoir [23], and more importantly, generates low-valence sulfur species on surface of lithium anode to induce uneven lithium deposition and massive generation of inactive lithium [24–26].

Employing weakly-solvating electrolyte is an effective strategy to suppress the shuttle effect and improve the * Corresponding authors at: Advanced Research Institute of Multidisciplinary Science, Beijing Institute of Technology, Beijing 100081, China.
Li–S battery cycling stability [31–33].

Generally, the weakly-solvating electrolytes protect the lithium anode without harming the sulfur redox kinetics under flooded elec­ trolyte conditions as the LiPSs are fully solvated to guarantee smooth sulfur redox kinetics [36,37].

Nevertheless, lean-electrolyte Li–S batteries suffer from highly sluggish sulfur redox kinetics due to high LiPS concentration or even LiPS saturation, and the actual performances are greatly degraded regarding the discharge ca­ pacity, cell polarization, and rate responses [41–44].

The above chal­ lenges are even more severe in weakly-solvating Li‒S batteries due to the lower solvating power of the electrolyte with low-DN co-solvents [45], leading to unexpected rapid cell failure due to the dramatic degradation of the sulfur redox kinetics [46–48].
Therefore, the lean-electrolyte con­ ditions have little effect on the thermodynamics of weakly-solvating Li‒ S batteries.

When the E/S ratio decreases from 12 to 6 μL mg−1, the discharge polarizations are basically not changed at around 100 mV at the Li2S nucleation stage (Figure S6), suggesting the electrolyte amount is enough for smooth cathode reactions within this flooded E/S ratio range.
Therefore, the sluggish ki­ netics of the discharge process, especially at the Li2S nucleation stage, is the main problem of weakly-solvating Li‒S batteries under leanelectrolyte conditions.
Therefore, the high kinetic polarization of weakly-solvating Li‒S batteries under lean-electrolyte conditions is resulted from the sluggish cathode kinetics.

The increased activation energy as the sulfur concentration increases demonstrates an exponen­ tial decline of the reaction rate coefficient under lean-electrolyte con­ ditions according to the Arrhenius equation.

In summary, ηac is the dominant kinetic polarization, and the interfacial charge transfer ki­ netics is confirmed as the critical limiting factor of weakly-solvating Li‒ S batteries under lean-electrolyte conditions.

The lower Li2S nucleation re­ action rate results in the Li2S nucleus changes from a diffusioncontrolled three-dimensional hemisphere-like morphology to a surface reaction-controlled two-dimensional needle-like morphology.

Controlled by the surface reaction, only a little amount of LiPS is able to be electrochemically reduced and form Li2S nuclei with smaller size on the conductive surface, which results in larger kinetic polarization to stabilize the small Li2S nuclei.
The thinner Li2S deposition layer at higher sulfur concentration is resulted from higher degree of surface reaction-controlled Li2S deposi­ tion and corresponding two-dimensional Li2S deposition.
Thinner deposition thickness brings more rapid conductive surface coverage by the insulating Li2S deposits, thereby blocking the subsequent reactions.

Therefore, the surface reaction controlled Li2S nucleation and growth under lean-electrolyte working conditions leads to rapid conductive surface coverage, premature termination of Li2S deposition, enlarged concentration polarization, and consequent discharge capacity degradation in weakly-solvating Li–S batteries (Fig. 3e).

This work reveals the surface reaction-controlled Li2S deposition kinetics as the origin of discharge capacity degradation of weakly-solvating Li‒S bat­ teries under lean-electrolyte working conditions.
Li salt anions are able to coordinate with LiPSs and are expected to accelerate the sulfur redox kinetics in weakly-solvating electrolyte under lean-electrolyte conditions [54–56].
Therefore, the LiFSI electro­ lyte successfully accelerates the interfacial charge transfer kinetics of weakly-solvating Li–S batteries under lean-electrolyte conditions.
The LiTFSI electrolyte can hardly guarantee smooth sulfur redox kinetics at high current density, and the Li‒S cells with the LiTFSI electrolyte fail immediately at 0.2 C.

In comparison, the Li‒S pouch cell with the LiTFSI electrolyte fails rapidly at 0.05 C and the discharge capacity is less than 200 mAh g−1 at higher rates due to the sluggish kinetics (Figure S41). 5 Ah Li‒S pouch cells with the LiFSI electrolyte were assembled and a high discharge capacity of 1150 mAh g−1 is delivered, which is 855 mAh g−1 higher than that in the LiTFSI electrolyte (Figure S42).

Therefore, Li‒S batteries with both high energy density and long cycling lifespan can be achieved by the LiFSI electrolyte that effectively accelerates the sulfur redox kinetics in weakly-solvating Li–S batteries under lean-electrolyte conditions. 3.

The term Ak2 indicates the deposition kinetics of Li2S and can be used to measure the relative speed of electrode passivation.[12a] The deposition nucleation rate of Li2S in DD electrolyte is nearly 5–6 times than that in the high-DN solvent based electrolytes (Figure 3i), implying that the insulating Li2S can rapidly cover the electrode surface and hinder their further deposition.

Among the electrolytes with high-DN co-solvents, the DD_ DMSO shows almost marginal Ak2 so that the extremely slow growth rate limits the deposition of Li2S, which is attributed to the greater kinetic barrier for the nucleation on the conductive electrode surface caused by the high Li2S solubility.[7] The DD_HMPA exhibits a moderate Li2S nucleation and growth rate, which accounts for the optimized 3D Li2S morphology with small granules and the suppressed electrode passivation.

Furthermore, the Li2S deposition in the DD electrolyte follows a hybrid model between the two-dimensional instantaneous (2DI) and three-dimensional progressive (3DP) model (Figure 3a, inset) due to the enhanced Li2S solubility by the highly electron donating NO3 � , consistent with the observed smooth Li2S layer with scanning electron microscopy (SEM) imaging (Figure 3d).[8,12b] In this case, the subsequent growth of Li2S is controlled by the surface mass transport of electrodepositing species, and will consequently be impeded by the insulating Li2S layer.

In great contrast, the current response of the cell with the DD_HMPA electrolyte indicates a hybrid 3DP and 3DI (three-dimensional instantaneous) model, suggesting the Li2S growth is controlled by bulk diffusion and the HMPA facilitates a fast solution-mediated mechanism in SRR (Figure 3b, inset).

Our work highlights the fundamental chemical concept of tuning the solvation structure to simultaneously tame the SRR and LMA stability for metal-sulfur batteries wherein the electrode reactions are heavily coupled with electrolyte chemistry.

More critically, the stability with the lithium metal anodes (LMAs) imposes a conflicting requirement for the solvents, that is, the reactivity of solvents with LMAs increases significantly with the electron donicity, resulting in highly unstable interfaces and hence shortened cell life for HSEs with high-DN solvents.[13] Therefore, it is essential to design advanced electrolytes with regulated solvation structures which are compatible with LMAs while concurrently exhibiting the advantages of fast SRR kinetics for lean-electrolyte Li� S batteries.[14] In this study, we present a HSE featuring core–shell solvation structure which addresses the conflicting challenges by endowing both high stability for the [S3] *� radical and high electro(chemical) compatible with the LMA.

Results and Discussion The Solvation Structure We hypothesize that the way to solve the conflicting challenges of promoting radical formation and compatibility with LMA essentially relies on manipulation of the solvation structure of the HSE.

Our results suggest that the DD_HMPA electrolyte is an effective strategy to simultaneously facilitate SRR and stabilize the LMA, among reported HSEs (Table S1), demonstrating the prospects of the DD_HMPA electrolyte for practical Li� S batteries.

More critically, the stability with the lithium metal anodes (LMAs) imposes a conflicting requirement for the solvents, that is, the reactivity of solvents with LMAs increases significantly with the electron donicity, resulting in highly unstable interfaces and hence shortened cell life for HSEs with high-DN solvents.[13] Therefore, it is essential to design advanced electrolytes with regulated solvation structures which are compatible with LMAs while concurrently exhibiting the advantages of fast SRR kinetics for lean-electrolyte Li� S batteries.[14] In this study, we present a HSE featuring core–shell solvation structure which addresses the conflicting challenges by endowing both high stability for the [S3] *� radical and high electro(chemical) compatible with the LMA.

This challenge lies on the low sulfur utilization and fast capacity fading at low electrolyte-to-sulfur ratios (E/S ratios).[4] In fact, achieving high sulfur utilization under lean electrolyte conditions (E/S5.0 μLmgsulfur � 1) in the conventional etherbased moderately solvating electrolytes (MSEs) has been intangible due to the low solubility and poor reactivity of lithium polysulfides (LiPSs) at such conditions, which is originated from the abruptly degraded transport and reaction kinetics of electrolytes with high-concentration (even saturated) LiPSs, and from the premature electrode passivation by the Li2S formation upon discharge.[5] Using sparingly solvating electrolytes (SSEs) can shift the sulfur reaction pathway from a dissolution–precipitation reaction to a quasi-solid-solid reaction.

Solvents possessing a high Gutmann donor number (DN), including dimethylacetamide (DMA, 27.8 kcalmol� 1),[6] N-dimethylformamide (DMF, 26.6 kcalmol� 1),[7] dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, 29.8 kcalmol� 1),[8] and 1,3-dimethyl-2-imidazolidinone (DMI, 29 kcalmol� 1),[9] have been shown to inherently promote LiPSs’ solubility compared to the low DN counterparts.[9–10] Specifically, these highly solvating electrolytes (HSEs) with high-DN solvents not only improve the solubility of LiPSs (and Li2S),[7,11] but also promote the formation of [S3] *� radicals during SRR, which appears to facilitate the conversion between long-chain and short-chain LiPSs.[12] Therefore, the HSEs are expected to enable formation of highly reactive LiPSs catholyte solutions during the reaction at lean electrolyte conditions, as opposed to the saturated and sluggish LiPSs catholyte solutions formed in conventional ether-based MSEs.

This suggests that the intermolecular hydrogen bonding between phosphamide groups with the DOL/DME plays a decisive role in stabilizing the interface with LMA; indeed, with the HMPA buried within the first solvation shell, their direct contact and reactions with the LMAs would be suppressed.
The confinement of HMPA leads to suppressed contact reactions with LMA at the interface and improved LMA plating efficiency.

According to the Pearson’s HSAB theory, we hypothesize that the higher-DN solvents show stronger solvent-Li+ binding, and therefore the formed solvent-Li+ complex shows weaker Lewis acidity (softer Lewis acid), which in turn shows stronger binding with the soft Lewis base [S3] *� .

For example, HMPA, showing higher binding energy with Li+ than other solvents, greatly reduces the acidity of Li+ in the solution, which stabilizes the [S3] *�radicals by forming stable HMPA� Li[S3] * complex.
The prolonged presence of [S3] *� radicals would greatly enhance its redox-mediation effect on the SRR, and thereby improve the sulfur utilization under lean electrolyte conditions.

Lithium−sulfur (Li−S) batteries are promising nextgeneration rechargeable batteries with an ultrahigh theoretical energy density of up to 2600 W h kg−1.15−18 Soluble Li polysulfides (LiPSs) connect the solid charge and discharge products of S8 and Li2S in sulfur cathodes and serve as key intermediates.19−23 Ether-based electrolytes currently constitute the benchmark for Li−S battery research and applications, typically composed of 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) and 1,2- dimethoxyethane (DME).24−27 These mixed solvents dissolve massive LiPSs to guarantee smooth cathodic conversion kinetics and full delivery of high discharge capacity and energy density.28−31 However, the parasitic reactions between the LiPSs and Li metal anodes result in unsatisfactory cycling stability of Li−S batteries in DOL/DME-based electrolytes.32−35 Previous researches have demonstrated that employing weakly solvating electrolytes (WSEs) by incorporating weakly solvating solvents (WSSs) into the DOL/DME benchmark can effectively diminish the LiPS corrosion on Li metal anodes and enhance the cycling stability of Li−S batteries.36−39 Nevertheless, the WSEs inevitably retard the LiPS cathodic conversion kinetics, leading to deteriorated cell polarization, reduced discharge capacity, and low energy density at the pouch cell level.40−44 The current chemical understandings impute the above dilemma to the decreased LiPS solubility.45−47 However, molecular-level insights into the ESP and the solvation structure of the dissolved LiPSs remain elusive, though their importance has been widely acknowledged in prominently determining the electrochemical behaviors of both the sulfur cathode and the Li anode.48−50 A direct correlation between the ESP and the LiPS redox kinetics has not yet been established, resulting in the blindness of the WSE design in promoting Li−S battery performances.

This phenomenon further signifies that the charge-transfer limitation, rather than mass transport or electron−ion conduction, primarily restricts the LiPS conversion kinetics in WSE-based Li−S batteries.

The newly emerged Raman signal indicates that the WSS coordinates directly with Li ion beyond the transition point,55 demonstrating that the two-stage variation in the ESP observed in Figure 3B results from the changes in the microscopic solvation structure.

In stage II, with insufficient SSSs for full coordination of LiPSs and increased molecular entropy, the WSSs begin to enter the inner solvation shell and directly coordinate with LiPSs following the Li bond principle.60 These changes in the LiPS solvation structure induced by WSS coordination result in a two-stage variation in the ESP and further affect the LiPS kinetic behaviors in Li−S batteries.

The above results manifest that the chargetransfer kinetics of the LiPS homogeneous reactions become intrinsically more sluggish with reduced ESP once the WSSs penetrate the LiPS inner solvation shell.

Furthermore, the WSS coordination increases the charge-transfer energy barrier in these rate-determining steps, hindering the overall LiPS redox kinetics and enlarging the overpotential of the LiPS heterogeneous reactions in WSEs (e.g., 0.78, 0.82, and 1.05 V for the systems of 2DME, DME + DIPE, and 2DIPE, respectively).

Overall, based on the experimental and theoretical evaluations of both homogeneous and heterogeneous reactions, it is evident that direct coordination of WSS with LiPSs significantly lessens the ESP of the WSEs, which further reduces the intrinsic LiPS reactivity, hinders the cathodic charge-transfer kinetics, and sharply enlarges the cathodic activation polarization.

This low solubility of LiPSs would intensify the precipitation of short-chain LiPSs, especially at low E/S ratios (also known as lean electrolyte conditions), resulting in the premature formation of Li2S passivation layer upon discharge, which inevitably results in low practical capacity with low S utilization.26 Furthermore, the parasitic reactions between the shuttled LiPSs and LMA would shorten the cycle life of Li−S batteries.

The employment of sparingly solvating electrolytes can shift the S conversion pathway from a dissolution−precipitation reaction to a quasi-solid−solid reaction, which suppresses the solvation and shuttle of LiPSs, effectively extending the cycle life of Li−S batteries even under lean electrolyte conditions.27 Nevertheless, it inevitably Received: March 28, 2025 Revised: June 9, 2025 Accepted: July 24, 2025 Published: July 28, 2025 Letter http://pubs.acs.org/journal/aelccp © 2025 American Chemical Society 4004 https://doi.org/10.1021/acsenergylett.5c00974 ACS Energy Lett. 2025, 10, 4004−4012 Downloaded from pubs.​acs.​org/​aelccp/​article-pdf/​10/​8/​4004/​42282075/​nz5c00974.​pdf by TSINGHUA UNIV user on 21 September 2026

sacrifices the S cathode redox kinetics, resulting in large polarization, inferior rate capability, and low capacity.28,29 To promote the S cathode redox kinetics under lean electrolyte conditions, recently, highly solvating electrolytes based on solvents with high Gutmann donor number (DN) were proposed, such as N, N, N′, N′-tetramethylurea (TMU),30 N, N′-dimethylethyleneurea (DMEU),31 dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO),32 and 3-fluoropyridine (3-FPN),22 which possesses strong electron-donating ability to regulate the solvation structure of LiPSs as well as promotes the solubility of LiPSs (Table S1).

Furthermore, high DN solvents can provide an additional disproportionation pathway of LiPSs by triggering the formation of trisulfur radical anion (S3 •−) intermediate, leading to the radical-assisted conversion pathway for LiPSs with rapid conversion kinetics.33 Moreover, in contrast to the twodimensional (2D) deposition morphology of Li2S in moderately/sparingly solvating electrolytes, the highly solvating electrolyte bestows the Li2S with a three-dimensional (3D) deposition morphology, which offers more assessable surface area for the reversible conversion between LiPSs and Li2S, leading to high capacity with high S utilization.

Unfortunately, high DN solvents with high electron donicity significantly increases the reactivity toward LMAs, which quickly consumes the limited Li source and hence shortens the cycle life.34 Therefore, promoting the S cathode redox kinetics while improving LMA compatibility simultaneously is essential to achieving high-capacity and long-cycling Li−S batteries, which is unattainable for current electrolyte design, especially under lean electrolyte conditions.

Although the DMEU molecule with a cyclic structure possesses better Li compatibility compared to that of noncyclic high DN solvents, its high donicity nature still makes it tend to react with LMA, and the battery life was limited to a few tens of cycles.31 To address this dilemma, we revisit the solvation structure of highly solvating electrolyte and molecule structure of DMEU.

This was ascribed to the weak electron donicity and low dipole moment (μ) of DOL (DN: 17.5 kcal mol−1, μ: 1.19 D) and DME (DN: 20.0 kcal mol−1, μ: 1.72 D), which exhibits moderately solvating ability with LiPSs, resulting in low solubility of LiPSs and sluggish S redox kinetics with unfavorable 2D Li2S deposition (Figures 1a and S1).

(b) For E-EDD electrolyte, the introduction of DMEU cosolvent with high DN and high μ significantly enhances the solvation of LiPSs and triggers S3 •−−based conversion pathway, leading to improved redox kinetics with 3D Li2S deposition morphology, while the existence of free DMEU solvent with high reactivity leads to poor Li compatibility.

(c) In E-PDD electrolyte, by tuning the molecular structure from five-membered cyclic DMEU to a six-membered cyclic DMPU, the DN and μ were further increased to achieve a DMPU-dominated inner solvation shell, which not only further promotes the conversion kinetics, but also minimizes free DMPU in the electrolyte to alleviate parasitic reactions with LMA.

This different intensity of S3 •−among EDD with PDD can be explicated by the Pearson’s hard and soft acid−base theory, where a soft acid (hard acid) predisposes to bind soft base (hard base).39 DMPU with strong coordination with Li+ delivers a higher-level of soft acidity than DMEU, inducing better stabilization of S3 •−(soft base).

For 0.1 M Li2S6 + 1.0 M LiTFSI in PDD solution, the S6 2−strongly interacts with Li+ and DMPU within 4.2 Å, validating the DMPU-dominated inner-solvation shell of Li2S6 (Figures 3a and 3d), where the DMPU solvent with high electron donicity is expected to promote the conversion kinetics of LiPSs.41 In sharp contrast, for 0.1 M Li2S6 + 1.0 M LiTFSI in EDD solution, the S6 2−tends to interact with both DMEU and DME, leading to a DMEU/DME-dominated innersolvation shell with limited conversion kinetics improvement (Figures 3b and 3e).

Since only part of the DMEU solvent is involved in the solvation shell, there are some parts of DMEU molecules that inevitably exist in a free state in the solution, which leads to the parasitic reactions with Li-metal.

Thereafter, the overpotential sharply increases for the cell using E-EDD, which was ascribed to the accumulation of thick byproducts and dead Li resulting from the continuous parasitic reaction between the DMEU solvent and LMA.
While the cycling life was extended to about 1000 h for the cell using E-DD, owing to the absence of corrosive DMEU solvent (Figure S10a).

The Li-metal cycled in E-EDD and E-DD shows obvious cracks with porous mossy-like morphology (Figures 4b and S10b), whereas that in E-PDD delivers smooth and uniform morphology (Figure 4c), indicating superior Limetal compatibility possessed by the DMPU solvent.

Moreover, the Tafel plot shows that the exchange current density of E-PDD (0.52 mA cm−2) is much higher than that of E-EDD (0.42 mA cm−2) and E-DD (0.12 mA cm−2) electrolyte (Figure S11a), benefiting from rapid Li+ transport kinetics in E-PDD (Figure S11b), which can eliminate the local aggregation of Li+ and suppress the growth of Li dendrites.45,46 To understand the origin of better Li-metal compatibility in the DMPU-based highly solvating electrolyte, the Gibbs free energy changes (ΔG) of DMPU and DMEU reacting with Limetal were calculated through density functional theory (DFT).

The E-PDD electrolyte shows higher ionic conductivity (11.3 mS cm−1) than E-EDD (10.3 mS cm−1) and E-DD (8.5 mS cm−1), which could availably reduce the concentration polarization and enable fast mass transport, resulting in a higher exchange current density.
Moreover, during the process of plating/stripping, uncoordinated DMEU in E-EDD electrolyte would spontaneously react with LMA, accelerating the generation of dead Li as well as uneven Li deposition.
As shown in Figures 4d and 4e, the ΔGDMPU (−3.1 eV) is lower than that of ΔGDMEU (−3.7 eV), indicating that the DMPU solvent exhibits lower reactivity toward Li-metal compared to that of DMEU.

This validates that the six-membered cyclic DMPU molecule exhibits smaller ring strain than DMEU molecule, which improves its intrinsic stability thermodynamically, thereby weakening the reactivity of DMPU solvent with LMA.

In addition, as has been demonstrated in the Raman, MD, and NMR studies, most of the DMPU solvent was strongly coordinated with Li+ to form DMPU-dominated inner-solvation shell, which minimizes the free DMPU in the electrolyte to alleviate parasitic reactions with LMA kinetically.

First, the systematical evaluation of Li2S deposition using various electrolytes was shown in Figures S13−22 and Table S4, which demonstrates that the DMPU-dominated inner solvation shell from E-PDD electrolyte can remarkably induce 3D Li2S deposition.

Furthermore, the cell with E-PDD is still able to retain 1079 mAh g−1 (77% of the capacity retention) after 135 cycles with low voltage polarization (Figure S23), whereas both cells using E-EDD and E-DD fail within 130 cycles due to a serious parasitic reaction between the solvent/LiPSs and LMAs.

As shown in the voltage profiles in Figure 5b, the discharge capacity difference among these three electrolytes was mainly attributed to their distinct capacity difference at the low plateau, which are 937 mAh g−1 (E-PDD), 785 mAh g−1 (E-EDD), and 577 mAh g−1 (E-DD), respectively.

This could be attributed to the high solubility of LiPSs and formation of an S3 •− intermediate in the highly solvating electrolyte, which induces the 3D electrodeposition of Li2S to access more capacity.

Moreover, as shown in Figures S24−25, both the shuttle constant (ks) and shuttle current measurements further confirmed that the DMPU-dominated inner-solvation shell of LiPSs in the E-PDD electrolyte availably restricts the casual diffusion of LiPSs to LMA and enables effective S-based redox conversion.

Therefore, the E-PDD electrolyte not only facilitates the conversion of LiPSs and regulates the electrodeposition of Li2S that results in high capacity with high S utilization but also suppresses the parasitic reaction with LMA and enables uniform Li plating/stripping, which bestows the Li−S battery with high capacity and good cycling stability.
The charge−discharge profiles show a much lower voltage polarization in the E-PDD electrolyte after 100 cycles, indicating superior S redox kinetics (Figure S31b).

In stark contrast, the Li||S cell using E-DD electrolyte displays rapid capacity decay with only 23% capacity retained after 80 cycles, which could be ascribed to the severe parasitic reaction between shuttled LiPSs and LMA as well as premature Li2S passivation.

As shown in Figure S14b, the Li2S deposition in E-PDD is highly consistent with the 3DI model, which was mainly attributed to the following two reasons: 1) the DMPU solvent initiates S3•−–based conversion pathway that facilitates the fast conversion kinetics, and 2) the high Li2S solubility in PDD (i.e., 0.55 mM, Figure S16) can instantaneously bestow abundant nucleation sites on cathode interfaces upon reaching its saturation limit.

Although the E-EDD could also trigger the S3•−–based conversion pathway to promote the conversion kinetics of LiPSs and 3D deposition of Li2S, the inferior solubility of Li2S in EDD (i.e., 0.25 mM, Figure S16) results in the progressive precipitation of the Li2S accompanied with the collision of Li2S particles, which follows closely with the 3DP model (Figure S14e), leading to a 3D island-like morphology with uneven Li2S granules (Figures S14f and S15b).
As a result, the moderate capacity was obtained in the E-EDD.

In contrast, owing to the very low solubility of LiPSs in E-DD electrolyte that produces nucleation site at the very early stage, of which the premature nucleation process follows a 2DI model (Figure S14h), leading to densely surface passivation of insulating Li2S with film-like morphology (Figures S14i and S15c).
This consequently hinders the conversion of LiPSs and results in very low capacity.

In addition, owing to the strong affinity between Li2S nuclei and LiPSs in high DN electrolyte with low diffusion barrier,23-24 the later formed Li2S will be preferentially deposited on the surface of early Li2S nuclei, resulting in 3D growth with porous structure.

The cell using E-PDD shows an extremely high dissolution capacity of 956 mAh g−1, which is markedly higher than those using E-EDD and E-DD, demonstrating that 3D porous Li2S deposition offered by DMPU is beneficial for enabling the reversible conversion of solid Li2S to liquid LiPSs.

When fully discharged to 1.7 V at stage (iv), owing to the formation of large porous Li2S deposits, the rapid migration of both electrons and ions was largely preserved, and thus the impedance still remains relatively low.

The E-EDD with a progressive Li2S nucleation process results in inhomogeneous Li2S deposits that continuously covers on the carbon fiber surface, which impedes the transport of electrons and ions to a certain extent, thus exhibiting the intermediate impedances.

For the cells using E-DD, this was ascribed to low solubility of LiPSs that leads to the early nucleation of Li2S, resulting in compact and film-like Li2S passivation layer, which hinders the continuous reduction of LiPSs to Li2S that results in low capacity.
In addition, when fully charged to 2.8 V at stage (vii), only a few S deposits was observed on the carbon fiber, implying severe active S material loss with low utilization.

The average shuttle current (ASC) of the cell using E-PDD (0.017 mA cm−2) was significantly smaller than the other two cells using E-EDD (0.022 mA cm−2) and E-DD (0.036 mA cm−2), which can be attributed to the following two reasons: (i) the DMPU solvent with high electron donicity is beneficial for producing S3•− intermediate that boosts the conversion kinetics of LiPSs to Li2S, leaving the LiPSs short time to approach the separator; (ii) the DMPU-dominated inner-solvation shell accompanied with DOL/DME-rich outer-solvation shell forms the wrapped-like structure of LiPSs, which could restrict the random migration of LiPSs to the separator.

The theoretical and experimental studies have demonstrated that the DMPU with high electron donicity strongly coordinates with Li+ to form the DMPU-dominated inner-solvation shell, which effectively regulates the solvation of lithium polysulfides (LiPSs) to initiate a S3 •−radical-assisted conversion pathway and 3D deposition behavior of Li2S, facilitating the S redox kinetics and utilization under leanelectrolyte conditions.

Furthermore, in addition to the strong confinement of DMPU in the inner-solvation shell that minimizes their contact with LMA to suppress their parasitic reactions kinetically, the DMPU solvent featured with sixmembered ring bears small ring strain to weaken their reactivity with LMA thermodynamically, thus enabling highly reversible Li plating/stripping over 1400 h.

However, due to the relatively large E/S ratio and the considerable distance between the positive and negative electrodes in the aforementioned H-type battery, the phase separation behavior of the electrolyte may be subject to certain disturbances.

This indicates that during the depth discharge, the decrease in soluble LiPSs concentration allows the electrolyte to restore its initial homogeneous state.

This morphological contrast directly verifies that CPME addition effectively inhibits chemical corrosion of SEI by polysulfides, thereby promoting uniform Li deposition and enhancing interfacial stability.

This compositional difference confirms that the CPME phase suppresses LiPSs migration to the anode and subsequent decomposition via physical blocking, constructing a sulfurlean, highly stable SEI structure.[32] Time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (TOF-SIMS) depth profiling further validates SEI compositional differences (Figure 4g,h).

Concurrently, intensified F−fragment signals in CPME/DME indicate anion (TFSI−)-dominated solvation promotes inorganic-rich SEI formation.[33] This anion-derived interphase exhibits high ionic conductivity and mechanical stability, synergistically suppressing dendrite growth and polysulfide parasitic reactions.

Comparative C2HO−fragment distribution analysis reveals high organic content in DOL/DME derived SEI originates from continuous reductive decomposition of solvents, accelerating irreversible electrolyte consumption.
In contrast, CPME/DME system suppresses solvent decomposition pathways, tailoring SEI composition toward inorganic salt-dominated stable structures.

These results demonstrate that the introduction of CPME significantly reduces side-reaction activity at the electrolyte-Li metal interface by reconstructing solvation microenvironments, providing critical guarantees for longterm cycling stability in Li-S batteries.

Meanwhile, on the Li metal anode side, due to the presence of phase separation behavior in the CPME/DME electrolyte, less change in colour was observed compared to the DOL/DME electrolyte, which proved the inhibition of LiPSs shuttle.

By comparing the state of the Li metal electrode after discharge, it was found that the Li metal in the DOL/DME electrolyte turned significantly black, while in the CPME/DME electrolyte, the Li metal still maintained its metallic luster.
This further proves the beneficial effect of the CPME/DME electrolyte in inhibiting the corrosion of the Li metal electrode.

At the Li metal anode, the weakly solvating CPME phase suppresses LiPSs diffusion via physical blocking while inducing inorganic-rich SEI formation, significantly enhancing Li deposition uniformity and interfacial stability.

Introduction Amidst the urgent global demand for energy transition and carbon neutrality, developing novel energy storage technologies with ultrahigh energy density has emerged as a frontier challenge in energy science.[1,2] The lithiumsulfur (Li-S) battery system, leveraging its unique dual-highcapacity electrode characteristics of sulfur cathode (1675 mAh g−1) and Li anode (3860 mAh g−1), demonstrates a superior theoretical gravimetric energy density of 2,600 Wh kg−1, positioning it as a transformative system to surpass current energy storage limits.[3,4] The competitiveness of Li-S batteries stems from resource substitution of critical metals, compared to layered oxide cathodes reliant on lowabundance cobalt/nickel, sulfur offers a disruptive advantage through its high natural abundance and low cost.[5,6] However, the polysulfide (LiPSs) shuttle effect creates orders-ofmagnitude gaps between theoretical and practical cycling stability/discharge capacity, constituting the primary technical barrier to industrialization.[7,8] Distinct from the intercalation mechanism in conventional lithium-ion batteries, the unique solid (S8)-liquid (LiPSs)- solid (Li2S2/Li2S) multiphase reaction pathway of Li-S batteries dictates dual regulation characteristics of redox kinetics.[9,10] In the electrolyte with high LiPSs solubility, while rapid liquid-phase polysulfide conversion enhances sulfur cathode kinetics, it inevitably intensifies LiPSs diffusion toward the Li anode, triggering dual detrimental consequences.

Research Article interphase (SEI) thickening and structural degradation, while irreversible active material depletion coupled with accelerated Li dendrite growth synergistically promote system failure.[11–13] Conversely, in the electrolyte with low LiPSs solubility, although physical confinement suppresses LiPSs shuttling, excessively sluggish liquid-phase reactions lead to incomplete LiPSs conversion, forming dense Li2S passivation layers on electrodes that deactivate reactive sites and induce drastic capacity fading.[14–17] This inherent cathode/anode interfacial behavior conflict fundamentally exposes conventional electrolyte design flaws in Li-S systems, urgently necessitating novel strategies to concurrently achieve rapid cathode kinetics and stable anode interphases.[18] To address these challenges, current electrolyte engineering focuses on solvation structure modulation to establish dynamic equilibrium between efficient sulfur conversion and polysulfide diffusion suppression.[19,20] Zhang et al. proposed an encapsulated polysulfide electrolyte (EPSE) employing concentric dual-solvation shells of LiPSs, inner high-solvation 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME) maintaining dissolution-precipitation balance, outer lowsolvation diisopropyl ether (DIPE) creating diffusion barriers, achieving good balance of cathode kinetics and anode stability.[21] Subsequent work optimized EPSE using 1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl-2,2,3,3-tetrafluoropropyl ether (HFE), constructing HFE-EPSE hybrid electrolytes that leveraged solvation free-energy gradients to elucidate medium solvation strength’s critical role in balancing Li deposition kinetics and sulfur conversion efficiency.[22] Although above studies establish a theoretical framework for LiPSs solvation regulation, the weakened solubility of LiPSs in the homogeneous electrolyte inevitably reduces the conversion kinetics of the sulfur cathode, resulting in the adverse passivation of partial sulfur site during long-term cycling.

Herein, guided by the idea of regulating the state of reactive species, we developed a novel electrolyte with low salt concentration (1 mol L−1) and low density (1.1 g cm−3) by employing 1,2- dimethylbenzene (DTL) and 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME) as solvents and achieved a clustered polysulfides-mediated sulfur conversion mechanism.

Herein, guided by the idea of regulating the state of reactive species, we developed a novel electrolyte with low salt concentration (1 mol L−1) and low density (1.1 g cm−3) by employing 1,2- dimethylbenzene (DTL) and 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME) as solvents and achieved a clustered polysulfides-mediated sulfur conversion mechanism.

The encapsulation effect of DTL with the ligand-mediated action of bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (TFSI−) drives the formation of polysulfide clusters in the electrolyte, thus realizing a clustered polysulfide encapsulation mechanism intermediate between the conventional solidliquid dissolution mechanism and the quasi-solid-solid conversion mechanism.

During sulfur conversion in ether electrolytes, the high-LPSs-content catholyte significantly decreases Li+ conductivity and deteriorates wettability.

The hybrid solid/solvating mechanism brings about fast conversion kinetics and avoids high-LPSs-content catholyte, as formed in the traditional DOL/DME-based electrolytes, which kinetically impedes the conversion process under lean and locally lean electrolyte conditions.

Introduction Lithium-sulfur (Li-S) battery based on the conversion chemistry of 2Li + S →Li2S delivers an ultrahigh theoretical energy density of 2600 Wh kg1.[1–7] However, in practical terms, its available energy density is low because the operation of Li-S batteries in the mainstream dioxolane/dimethoxyethane (DOL/DME) electrolyte requires a high electrolyte/sulfur (E/S) ratio (usually >5 μL mg1).[8–12] DOL and DME with high donor numbers show high dissolution of the Li polysulfides (LPSs); therefore, the 1M ether electrolyte participates in the “dissolution-precipitation” conversion process at the cathode side and converts to catholyte after dissolving LPSs.[13,14] Under lean-etherelectrolyte conditions, our previous work revealed that S cathodes suffer from sluggish conversion kinetics caused by significantly decreased Li+ conductivity and deteriorated wettability of the high-LPSs-ratio catholyte.[15] In addition to low gravimetric energy density, the volumetric energy density of Li-S batteries is largely limited by the demand for high-porosity (>70%) S cathodes.[16] A dense S cathode fails to work in conventional ether electrolytes because it undergoes a locally low E/S ratio with a decreased electrolyte uptake in the cathode structure.

S1d), lean electrolyte transforms to a gel-like catholyte after dissolving a high content LPSs [S2, S3], and it undergoes a significant decrease in Li+ conductivity, along with severe deterioration in wettability to the cathode and the separator, which subsequently lead to the failure of the Li-S cell.

A dense cathode with limited pore volume only adsorbs a small amount of electrolyte within the electrode structure, and forms a locally low E/S ratio condition, which subsequently leads to cathode deterioration and battery failure.
Similarly, dense S cathodes are also capable to work at locally lean electrolyte conditions benefited from the unique S conversion mechanism in the 1M MAN electrolyte as shown in Figure 5f.
The reduced LPSs solubility mitigates the deterioration of electrolyte solvation structure and physical properties caused by LPSs dissolution during discharge.

Coupled with MAN’s inherent high relative permittivity, the 1M MAN electrolyte maintains its fast Li+ conductivity and good wettability during S conversion, thereby establishing the foundation for leanelectrolyte operation.

Therefore, S cathodes in 1M MAN electrolyte perform a hybrid conversion process (Figure 5e) with solid S to solvated LPSs, as well as solid S to solid LPSs, substantially reducing electrolyte involvement during redox reactions, ensuring a complete conversion under lean-electrolyte conditions.

The hybrid solid/solvating conversion pathway contributes to well-maintained high ionic conductivity and good wettability of the electrolyte during the conversion process, successfully circumventing the dependence of battery performance on electrolyte dosage.
However, when applying the 1M MAN electrolyte, the overpotential is even lower than the 1M DOL/DME electrolyte at the first discharge plateau, indicating more favorable conversion dynamics.
Besides, GITT profiles demonstrate the 1M MAN electrolyte provides the fastest conversion kinetics among the three electrolytes.
The above results demonstrate the 1M MAN electrolyte alters the conversion mechanism of S cathodes and enables fast conversion kinetics.
The Li-S battery with the G20.8LiTFSI electrolyte unsurprisingly shows high overpotentials during the whole discharge process, owing to the slow solid conversion pathway and low Li+ conductivity.
As for the 1M DOL/DME electrolyte, it is widely accepted to afford fast redox Li-S chemistry with the mediation effect of solvated LPSs, and the corresponding GITT profile shows low overpotential.
This conversion mechanism offers fast kinetics because the solvated LPSs function as mediators to promote redox reactions.
One is that the conversion process from solid S to solid LPSs without the mediation of solvated LPSs is kinetically slow.

The sluggish kinetics in sparingly solvating electrolytes leads to unsatisfying cyclability and poor rate performance.[42] Besides, sparingly solvating electrolytes are costly due to their high content Li salts, which makes them difficult to be used in large scale.

However, the “dissolution” process fundamentally requires a high E/S ratio (usually >5 μL mg1) to fully dissolve LPSs intermediates, leading to a significant reduction in the overall energy density of Li-S batteries as shown in Figure S1, Supporting Information.
Combining the in-situ Raman characterizations on cathodes and electrolyte, it demonstrates a hybrid conversion process in the 1M MAN electrolyte with S converting to both solvated and solid LPSs.

Pairing the galvanostatic intermittent titration technique (GITT) with EIS is an effective approach to study cell polarization.[40] By applying this GITT-EIS method to Li || S cells with practical sulfur loading, the overall cell polarization (ηtotal) can be resolved into three contributions: ohmic (ηohm), activation (ηact), and concentration (ηconc) polarizations. ηohm captures ionic resistance in the bulk electrolyte as well as electronic and contact resistances within the electrodes and cell hardware; it can be extracted from the high-frequency intercept on the Nyquist plot. ηact corresponds to the energy barrier of the interfacial charge-transfer process and, together with ηohm, produces the instantaneous voltage jump observed whenever the current is stepped during GITT measurement.

For both the cell with MSE-MtBE and DOL/DME electrolyte, the resulting ηtotal shows a gradual increase at the beginning of the discharge and peaks at ∼25% depth of discharge (DOD) when Li2S/Li2S2 starts to nucleate (Figures 3g and S16a).

MSEs show significantly lower Rct compared to DOL/DME, resulting from the weakened Li+-solvent interactions discussed before.
This leads to easier desolvation and explains faster redox kinetics at the Li metal anode.

This suggests that, even in MSEs, the main energy barrier for desolvation is still coming from the dissociation of the Li+-DME pairing, while the factors like total number of strongly bound DME affects the pre-exponential factor in the Arrhenius equation and the overall Rct.

Note that MtBE indeed presents the smallest activation energy, proving its effectiveness in reducing not only the quantity, but also the strength of Li+-DME pairing through solvent-solvent interactions.
It weakens excessive Li+-solvent binding and promotes favorable cationanion contacts, leading to reduced desolvation barrier and superior anode performance.

As a result, the desolvation barrier for Li+ ion is reduced and an inorganic-enriched solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) is formed on the anode surface, leading to a better reversibility of Li plating and stripping (Figure 1a).
This confirms the formation of a more stable SEI with MSE-MtBE, which in turn enhances the stability of Li-metal anode.
On the other hand, the DOL/DME electrolyte leads to the formation of more reduced sulfur species, indicating a greater degree of LiPS shuttling to the anode.

Due to the reduction of LiPS solubility and regulation of solvation structures, the LiPS shuttling effect is expected to be effectively mitigated in MSE-MtBE, which could make a substantial impact on the cyclability of Li–S cells.
In contrast, the MSE-MtBE cell shows much slower current change, and the shuttle current stabilizes at ∼0.013 mA, demonstrating its ability to suppress shuttling.

The resulting ηohm for the MSE-MtBE cell is slightly greater than the DOL/DME cell due to their ionic conductivity difference, with both cells exhibiting a peak value at the nucleation point (2.81 mV for MSE-MtBE and 2.10 mV for DOL/DME) when LiPS concentration reaches its maximum.

The MSE-MtBE cell shows a greater ηact at the Li2S/Li2S2 nucleation point (19.5 mV) compared to the baseline cell (10.4 mV), likely because of reduced LiPS concentration in MSE-MtBE, leading to fewer nuclei and nucleation sites.
In fact, the ηconc in MSE- MtBE has a peak value of 44.7 mV at ∼25% DOD, which is lower than that in DOL/DME (47.4 mV).
This is likely due to easier LiPS movement and lower desolvation energy in MSE-MtBE, aligning well with the previous discussion.

Additionally, during termination of discharge, most of the electrochemically active surface is covered; the MSE-MtBE cell shows significantly lower ηconc compared to the baseline cell, thanks to its better wettability and potentially more uniform deposition in the electrode (Figure S17).
As shown in Figure S18, the MSE-MtBE cell achieves a higher response current peak and a larger Li2S deposition capacity of 232 mA h g−1, compared to 161 mA h g−1 for the DOL/DME cell.
This leads to higher discharge capacity and active material utilization in actual Li || S cells.
However, in a practical cell with high sulfur loading and low E/S ratio, the nucleation process can also be affected due to polysulfide solubility differences, as discussed in the previous section.

This suggests that the energy barrier for the charge-transfer process, which is likely associated with desolvation at the electrochemically active surface, is lower in MSE-MtBE, whereas the overall reaction rate is slower, plausibly due to the lower conductivity of MSE-MtBE (Figure S21).

Additionally, in the CV curves of Li2S6 symmetric cells, MSE-MtBE shows slightly lower, but more reversible response current, suggesting fewer side reactions and better stability of the conversion process (Figure S22).

Note that α-S8 tends to form when the reaction kinetics move toward solid-state conversion.[32,45] This two-step sulfur deposition process could be characteristic in the MSE due to lower LiPS solubility and regulated solvation properties.
This mechanism may be pivotal toward maintaining adequate charging kinetics, while minimizing LiPS dissolution in MSEs.
The increased capacity and capacity retention may benefit from reduced polysulfide dissolution and regulated solvation.
These results reveal that the addition of MtBE plays an important role in improving the capacity and cyclability of Li– S cells, which may be attributed to its influence on both the electrodes.

From the voltage profile in Figure 5e, the cell never reaches 2.8 V before the time cutoff, likely due to severe LiPS shuttling resulting from higher polysulfide solubility, faster migration, and its faster reaction with Li metal at higher temperatures.

Moreover, stable CEs with an average of 94.6% are achieved throughout the cycles, highlighting the effective suppression of polysulfide shuttling and side reactions in the MSE-MtBE electrolyte even under harsh conditions.
This suggests some degree of correlation between solvation structure and cycling performance as the CEs of different electrolytes match the sequence of chemical shifts in Li NMR.
This can be attributed to the mitigated LiPS shuttling and more complete sulfur conversion, agreeing well with the operando XRD results discussed earlier.
They could also arise from anode-cathode crosstalk owing to the stronger solvating power of the baseline electrolyte.

These results indicate that MSE-MtBE most effectively shifts polysulfide solvation toward more ion pairing, which could directly affect polysulfide migration and conversion; accordingly, MSE-MtBE was selected for further evaluation.

These higher diffusivities with the addition of MtBE likely arise from the overall reduced solvent-Li+ binding, as well as the low viscosity of MtBE, which promotes faster mass transport in the actual cells for MSEs.

Additionally, stronger peaks of oxidized sulfur species (─SOx) were detected on the DOL/DME-derived cathode, which may originate from unwanted decomposition of electrolyte components and their reactions with sulfur species.

In contrast, free MeTHF is observed in LiTFSI: CSA: MeTHF = 1:4:6 and 1:6:6 electrolytes.

These results demonstrate a unique solvation structure wherein CSA dominates the inner solvation shell and MeTHF occupies the outer solvation shell. 7Li NMR spectra reveal a pronounced upfield shift (i.e., shielding effect) with increasing CSA content, demonstrating enhanced electron density around Li nuclei due to strong CSA−Li+ coordination (Figure S11).
The 17O chemical shift of 0.1 M Li2S6 in CSA exhibits a significant upfield shift of −0.16 ppm, whereas that of 0.1 M Li2S6 in DME shows a smaller upfield shift (−0.11 ppm).
The 17O chemical shifts of 0.1 M Li2S6 in DOL and MeTHF exhibit slight upfield shifts (−0.03 and −0.01 ppm, respectively), indicating weak coordination with Li+.

This suggests that MeTHF is mostly located in the outer shell of Li2S6 solvation structure, forming a gradient distribution of mixed solvents. 0.1 M Li2S6 in the mixed solvents (CSA:MeTHF and DME:DOL) were further analyzed by comparative 7Li NMR spectroscopy (Figure 3e).
The shield effect of Li+ in CSA:MeTHF is stronger than in DME:DOL due to the stronger coordination capability of CSA compared to DME.

From the result of radial distribution function (RDF) in Figure S25a, the S6 2− exhibits a strong correlation peak with both Li+ and CSA within 4.5 Å in 0.2 M Li2S6 + 1.0 M LiTFSI in CSA:MeTHF solution, indicating that CSA occupies the inner solvation sheath of Li2S6.
In contrast, for 0.2 M Li2S6 + 1.0 M LiTFSI in DME:DOL solution, both DME and DOL occupy the solvation shell of S6 2−(Figures S25b−d).
Ten mM Li2Sx (x = 2, 4, 6, 8) in CSA:MeTHF (4:6 by molar) exhibits uniform a darkbrown color, indicating high LiPSs dissolubility.
In contrast, 10 mM Li2Sx in DME:DOL (1:1 by vol.) shows visible precipitate (the dotted box), indicating poor dissociation and low dissolubility of polysulfides (Sx 2−) species.
The sulfur atomic concentration ([S]) in a saturated Li2S6/CSA solution reaches approximately 18 mol L−1, which is significantly higher than that in DME (9 mol L−1; Figure S24).

Conversely, [S] in a saturated Li2S6/MeTHF solution is only 0.6 mol L−1, lower than that in DOL (1.0 mol L−1). 17O NMR spectroscopy was employed to characterize the LiPSs solvation structure (Figure 3a−d).
The ionic conductivity of 0.1 M Li2Sx in CSA:MeTHF is higher than that in DME:DOL (Figure S23).

Notably, 0.1 M Li2S6 in CSA:MeTHF exhibits a diffusion rate of Li+ (DLi +, sol.) of 3.1 × 10−10 m2 s−1, which is less than a half value measured in DME:DOL (6.3 × 10−10 m2 s−1).

This suggests a greater degree of aggregation occurs in the CSA:MeTHF electrolyte.

In addition to suppressing the LiPSs shuttle effect and stabilizing LMA by reducing parasitic reactions, we assume that the intrinsic CSA− MeTHF interaction triggers the formation of Li2S6 clusters, which also affect the reaction kinetics to promote 3D Li2S deposition.41,42 The viscosity of 0.1 M Li2S6 was measured to calculate the diffusion rate of Li2S6 (DLi2S6) using Einstein- Stokes eq (Figure 3i).43 Li2S6 in CSA:MeTHF shows a DLi2S6 of 2.3 × 10−11 m2 s−1, which is lower than that in DME:DOL (8.9 × 10−11 m2 s−1), confirming a slower diffusion process of Li2S6.

The Li+ diffusion coefficient (DLi+-CV) was calculated by linearly fitting Ip against the square root of the scan rate (v1/2) based on Randles-Sevcik equation in Figures S36 and S37.34 CSA/MeTHF electrolyte shows a higher value of DLi+-CV than DD electrolyte, indicating a rapid diffusion-controlled electrochemical processes and enhanced redox reaction kinetics.

The combination of midstrong/ weak solvation solvents endows a distinctly gradient lithium polysulfides (LiPSs) solvation structure, suppressing their shuttle effect and enhancing Li-metal compatibility.

The electrolyte formula combining midstrong solvation (2,5- dimethyl-1,2,5-thiadiazolidin 1-oxide, CSA) and weak solvation (2-methyltetrahydrofuran, MeTHF) solvents outperforms all other electrolyte formulations.

The CSA/MeTHF electrolyte, combining midstrong and weak solvation solvents, exhibits a distinct solvent−solvent interaction that forms a gradient solvation structure, as evidenced by multiple spectroscopic techniques.
Further, the electrolyte was prepared using an optimal molar ratio of LiTFSI:CSA:MeTHF = 1:4:6, with the detailed optimization shown in Figures S10 and S11.
Notably, LiTFSI: CSA: MeTHF = 1:4:6 electrolyte displays an excellent average CE (99.4%) with a high capacity retention (93%).
These results confirm that the distinctive solvation structure could simultaneously stabilize LMA and accelerate the LiPSs redox conversion kinetics.
Herein, we propose a solvent screening criterion using the dielectric constant (εr) and donor number (DN) as a synergistic descriptor.

Herein, we propose an electrolyte solvent screening criterion based on εr and DN, where 75 electrolyte solvents were classified and evaluated by using seven critical electrochemical performance parameters.

L ithium−sulfur (Li−S) batteries, featuring an ultrahigh theoretical energy density (up to 2600 Wh kg−1) and low cost, abundant S as the cathode material, are considered as the leading candidates for next-generation energy storage systems.1,2 However, their industrialization has been persistently hindered by critical challenges, among which electrolyte design and optimization play a pivotal role.3 The electrolyte serves as not only an ion-transport medium but also a core component, which profoundly governs the dissolution, diffusion, and conversion of lithium polysulfides (LiPSs) and critically impacts the stability of electrode−electrolyte interfaces.4 Benefiting from the prior lithium-ion battery technology, early research predominantly employed ether-based solvents, such as 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) and 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME) as the baseline electrolytes.5,6 Although ether solvents exhibit high solubility for LiPSs, which ensures favorable sulfur conversion kinetics, this property also causes the shuttle effect of LiPSs.7,8 Dissolved LiPSs species migrate between the cathode and anode, causing irreversible active material rapid loss and lithium metal anode (LMA) corrosion.9,10 Recently, various electrolyte strategies have been explored to suppress the shuttle effect of LiPSs.11,12 For instance, employing weak-solvating-power solvents, e.g., carbonates,13 single-oxygen ether,14 and hydrofluorinated ether,15 results in incomplete sulfur redox reactions and easy formation of passivation layer on the cathode surface.

Introducing ionic liquids or highly concentrated electrolytes effectively restricted LiPSs dissolution, however also leads to high viscosity, low ionic conductivity, and high costs.16,17 Although these approaches have achieved incremental progress, they often inevitably face a dilemma of trade-offs: suppressing shuttle effect of LiPSs comes at the expense of compromised conversion kinetics or interfacial stability.18 Then, to achieve a high S utilization under lean electrolyte condition, a series of Gutmann’s donor number (DN) solvents with strong-solvating-power are proposed to boost the solubility of LiPSs leading to a rapid conversion kinetics based on a solid−liquid−solid S redox process.19,20 From the perspective of electrolyte engineering, a fundamental understanding of the LiPSs’ solvation is essential for the industrialization of Li−S batteries.

These results can be attributed to the distinct solvent properties: (1) DMSO with strong solvation ability accompanies intrinsic corrosion, leading to short cycle life.

In this study, the design principle of moderately solvating electrolytes (MSEs) for LSBs is demonstrated by using a multiple-solvent system comprising of a highly solvating solvent, a weakly solvating solvent, and a non-solvating solvent to create a well-balanced electrolyte system.
To design feasible MSEs for LSBs, a multiple solvent system containing a highly solvating solvent, a moderately solvating solvent and a sparingly solvating solvent is selected in this work.

The LiPS solubility of this electrolyte system can be tuned to overcome both the low solubility problem (encountered in the electrolyte with moderately solvating solvent and sparingly solvating solvent) and the high solubility problem (fast dissolving and shuttling of LiPSs with highly solvating solvent).

Conclusion Inspired by the design of LHCEs for LMBs with conventional intercalation cathodes, a set of MSEs for LSBs has been designed by utilizing a ternary solvent system with a highly solvating solvent, a weakly solvating solvent, and a non-coordinating diluent.

In general, the liquid electrolytes for LSBs reported in literature can be grouped into three main categories: 1) highly solvating electrolytes (HSEs), 2) moderately solvating electrolytes (MSEs), and 3) sparingly solvating electrolytes (SSEs).[24,27] HSEs, such as the conventional ether-based electrolyte of 1 m Li bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI) in 1,2-dimethoxyethane and 1,3-dioxolane (DME/DOL, 1:1 by vol.) with additive Li LiNO3, emphasize on promoting PSs solubility and fast Li-S reaction kinetics with less electrolyte utilization, but in turn promoting PSs shuttling and causing poor Li metal stability and short cycle life.[28] On the other end of the spectrum, SSEs, such as high-concentration electrolytes (HCEs), localized high-concentration electrolytes (LHCEs)[29–31] and electrolytes with large molecule solvents or ionic liquids (ILs),[32–34] are designed to significantly reduce LiPSs solubility to inhibit LiPSs shuttling and subsequent parasitic reactions, but they reduce the overall cell capacity and cyclability due to the high viscosity or low ion conductivity, and poor conversion of PSs.[17] Very recently, MSEs have been reported to balance the advantages and issues existing in HSEs and SSEs, anticipating to be a medium of controlled PS solubility to inhibit the PSs shuttling effect without sacrificing the high S utilization and fast Li–S reaction kinetics required to enable a stable long-term cyclability of LSBs with a high discharge capacity.[27] However, how to design a wellbalanced MSE remains unclear. 2.

The rate performance results indicate that the conversion of the long-chain PSs to the short-chain PSs is the rate-limiting step during discharge that creates a large overpotential in the cell and causes the LSB to prematurely reach the cut-offvoltage specially at higher C rates at and above C/2, even at C/3 the dip at the start of second plateau reflects the kinetics issue for the formation of short-chain PSs in E-baseline.

Though the four DMFN electrolytes have lower ionic conductivity and higher viscosity than E-baseline (Figure 1b), which make the LSBs give lower discharge capacity in the initial cycles than E-baseline, they do have higher average Li CEs (Figure 1b) and much lower LiPS solubility (Figure S7a, Supporting Information) than E-baseline, which cause less side reactions between electrolyte and Li metal and much less loss of S active material from cathode and largely reduced crosstalk of LiPSs from cathode to anode.

In addition, the ionic conductivities of the DMFN electrolytes are still moderately high (≈6–7 mS cm−1), therefore the combination of these factors makes the DMFN electrolytes exhibit similar charge and discharge rate capabilities to E-baseline when the discharge rate is at or below C/3.

While Ebaseline had a higher initial capacity because of low viscosity and more wettability of cathodes, the DMFN electrolytes showed significantly improved cycling stability and CE, with the 0.8M- DMFN exhibiting the highest specific capacity among the DMFN electrolytes and the 1.0M-DMFN electrolyte the best cycling stability having a high-capacity retention of 81.3% (604 mAh g−1) after 300 cycles.

Over a period of 250 cycles, the voltage profiles of E-baseline containing LSBs showed significant growth in cell polarization, overcharging of the cells, and rapid capacity degradation after 100 cycles highlighting the high reactivity of Ebaseline with both S and Li electrodes.

Furthermore, the 0.8M-DMFN and E-baseline electrolytes were evaluated in 1-Ah pouch cells and the preliminary cycling results shown in Figure S18 (Supporting Information) also indicate the 0.8M-DMFN shows better cycling stability than E-baseline where the latter exhibits large overpotential after 40 cycles because the extra charging capacity from unwanted side reactions leads to low Coulombic efficiency ultimately to cell death.

The S electrode is inherently more reactive with the electrolyte compared to the conventional Li-ion intercalation cathodes due to the ability to continuously dissolve S and LiPSs, be suspended in the electrolyte, and migrate to and react with the LMA leading to irreversible loss of active materials, depletion of electrolyte and insulation of Li anode.

This phenomenon is prevalent in E-baseline due to its high solubility and reactivity with S and LiPSs.[24] It is well known that self-discharge is a big issue in LSBs with liquid electrolytes, resulting in poor calendar life of LSBs.[44] Therefore, to test the self-discharge of LSBs with Ebaseline and DMFN electrolytes at the charged state over 1-week intervals for a period of 28 weeks can give us the calendaring stability of LSBs with these electrolytes.

The apparent loss of the plateau in 2.4– 2.1 V during discharge, which corresponds to the voltage plateau of transferring Li2S8 to Li2S6 in a typical discharge process, in the E-baseline cell can attribute to the high solubility of Li2S8 in Ebaseline.

It is concluded that the suppression of LiPSs solubility and the more robust passivation layer on the S and Li electrodes, observed in the DMFN electrolytes, more effectively mitigate the S/LiPSs shuttling effect so that it suppresses the self-discharge of the LSBs during storage or calendar aging and improves the long-term health of the LSBs.[45,46] 2.3.

To gain insight on the utilization, speciation, and retention of S, LiPSs, and Li0 in LSBs after cycling in both Ebaseline and 1.0M-DMFN, the HPLC, UV–vis, GC-MS (HUGs) method developed by Meng and colleagues was employed.[47] As shown in Figure 4, retention for Li0 after 100 cycles reveals that 1.0M-DMFN cycled Li0 has a lower amount of irreversible Li0 consumption that is assigned to the side reactions in the formation of the SEI, Li2S, and Li2S2 and has improved the overall Li0 retention, corroborating the improved Li° conditions observed in the post-mortem characterization results.

On the other hand, when cycled in E-baseline, an HSE, the S was primarily converted to LiPSs and continuously dissolved in the electrolyte leading to continuous side reactions and accelerated loss of S from the electrode leading to poor CE and accelerated cell degradation. 2.4.

The higher Li CE and improved long-term cycling stability of the LSBs with 1.0M-DMFN electrolyte can be attributed to the suppressed LiPS shuttle effect which in turn improves the morphology of deposited LMA and minimizes its corrosion.

The F 1s spectra (Figure 5h) further reveal the significantly increased variety and intensity of fluorinated species in the SEI on LMA from the 1.0M-DMFN due to the inclusion of TFEO that has been reported to form a more homogeneous and F-rich SEI that enhanced the protection of and stability with Li metal during cycling.[40,48] A weaker intensity for LiPS species was measured on the surface of Li metal cycled in 1.0M-DMFN in the S 2p spectra along with a stronger intensity for peaks related to decomposed TFSI−byproducts that form a more robust, anionrich SEI layer (Figure 5i).
The lower intensity of LiPS species on the LMA from the 1.0M-DMFN cell further corroborates a reduction in LiPS dissolution and shuttling in the DMFN electrolytes in the LSBs.

The higher intensity N-S peak measured in the DMFN cycled LMA in the N 1s spectra (Figure S21, Supporting Information) corroborates a more inorganic SEI of decomposed TFSI−byproducts that further protects the LMA from corrosion while cycling.

The observed physical condition and chemical environment of the cycled LMA in 1.0M-DMFN demonstrates that the DMFN electrolyte significantly has enhanced compatibility with the LMA and reduced LiPS migration and parasitic reactions inhibiting the PS shuttle effect, thus mitigating the corrosion and inactivity of the LMA.

The XPS analysis of the DMFN cycled S electrode reveals a less prominent organic phase found in the C 1s (Figure 6a), a higher intensity of peaks decomposed TFSI−in the S 2p (Figure 6b), a slightly higher intensity of C–F and Li–F peaks in the F 1s spectra (Figure 6c) and a less prominent reduction of LiNO3 in the N 1s spectra (Figure 6d), indicating that the DMFN electrolyte promotes a more inorganic-rich cathode electrolyte interphase (CEI), unlike the more organic-rich and unstable CEI of the E-baseline cycled electrode.

The noticeably stronger C–C peak and the overall lower S intensity in the corresponding C 1s and S 2p spectra of the E-baseline cycled electrode may be attributed to the bare C substrate and S particle delamination observed in the SEM images of the cycled electrodes, shown in Figure S22b (Supporting Information), corroborating the accelerated degree of LiPS dissolution and migration in E-baseline.

The improved morphology, structural integrity, and CEI composition observed of the cycled S electrode in 1.0M-DMFN highlights the profound effect of the designed MSEs to reduce excessive LiPS dissolution and mitigate PS shuttling while cycling the LSB.

Further investigation utilizing in situ measurements[49,50] would be required to ascertain the mechanism of retaining α-S8 in the DMFN after cycling, however, this observation could be a factor demonstrating an enhanced reversibility of S8 during cycling or improving long-term stability and structural retention of the S-electrode in the designed DMFN MSEs. 3.

The reversible capacity remained larger than the discharge capacity of the Li–S battery (3.04 mAh cm−2), confirming that cell capacity is not limited by the remaining capacity of the LMA, consistent with the results reported in previous studies.[9] However, 21% loss in the LMA indicates significant LMA degradation over 46 cycles only, as supported by the thick, porous layer observed in the cross-sectional images of the cycled LMA (Figure 1e).
This demonstrates the significant decomposition of the solvents, rather than the salt anions, in the Li–S battery.

However, a certain amount of liquid electrolyte must be consumed for wetting the porous Li layer; therefore, the remaining amount of electrolyte was insufficient for stably operating the Li–S battery.
The cell was rejuvenated owing to electrolyte exchange (Figure 1g), which confirms that solvent depletion is responsible for cell degradation.
The electrolyte decomposition can be increased by roughening the LMA and trapping the electrolyte components in the porous layer.
The density and uniformity of the LMA morphology increased during cycles with the decrease in solvating power, thereby enhancing Li reversibility.
However, the reduction in solvating power adversely affected the liquid-phase reduction reaction of the LiPSs.

Upon comparing the residual electrolytes after operation with strongly and moderately solvating electrolytes, we identified electrolyte depletion as the root cause of cell failure in lean-electrolyte Li–S batteries, not only in conventional electrolytes but also in other types of electrolytes.
This issue was effectively mitigated by the altered SEI structure and Li morphology resulting from the changes in the solvation structure.
The main solvent with high solvating power predominantly coordinates with Li+, increasing the solubilities of LiPSs and aggravating Li corrosion.

When a cosolvent extracts electrons from the main solvent via solvent-cosolvent interactions, the solvating power of the main solvent reduces.[15a,21] Subsequently, anion coordination in the Li+ solvate increases, decreasing the solubilities of the LiPSs and increasing the stability of the LMA.

However, electrolytes with extremely low LiPS solubilities may hinder redox reactions at the cathode.[5b,7a] Therefore, electrolytes with moderate solvating power may impart long lifespans to lean-electrolyte Li–S batteries.
This can be explained by the similar ionic conductivities of the electrolytes when Li2S4 is present.
In the DME electrolyte, where Li2S4 has the highest solubility, the ionic conductivity decreases more significantly, likely due to increased viscosity.

The DME-TFOFE electrolyte exhibited a 20% smaller discharge capacity and a larger discharge overvoltage by 0.8 V than the DME electrolyte owing to the low LiPS solvating power of the former electrolyte.
The reduced PS shuttle currents of the DME-FE electrolytes with respect to that of the DME electrolyte are in agreement with their PS solubilities.
Interestingly, DME-TFOFE exhibited a slightly higher shuttle current than the moderately solvating electrolytes, despite having the lowest solvating power and PS solubilities.
This can be attributed to the stabilization of the PS monoanions with lower charge densities, possessing lower LUMO levels, in DME-TFOFE than the dianions (Figure S19, Supporting Information).
These species were more likely to be reduced at the LMA while dianions are more Adv.
