This early Li2S precipitation, observed as the solvating power of the electrolytes decreased, suggests that as the solvating power weakens, solid-phase conversion is favored over liquid-phase conversion, allowing Li2S to crystallize more readily.
This absence is attributed to high cell polarization and hindered oxidation reactions caused by the aggregation of LiPS on the cathode and separator (Figure S21, Supporting Information).
The large overpotential of the DME-TFOFE electrolyte reflects sluggish LiPS redox kinetics owing to low LiPS solvating power.
This demonstrates that a weakly solvating electrolyte causes severe LiPS aggregation, yielding a high overpotential and low discharge capacity under lean-electrolyte conditions.
This indicates that augmenting anion coordination to Li+ improves the stability of the LMA.

This finding is in accordance with those reported in previous studies on improved Li compatibility using a combination of an LiFSI salt and a weakly solvating solvent.[15] To investigate the correlation between LMA stability and lifespan of the Li–S cell under lean-electrolyte conditions, cycling stability tests were conducted on the electrolytes at an E/S ratio of 5 and a 0.15 C rate.

Despite having the highest LMA reversibility, the DME-TFOFE electrolyte exhibited poor cycling stability, indicating that the reversibility of the sulfur cathode determines the cycling stability when the solvating power of electrolyte is weak.

Except in the case of the DME-TFOFE electrolyte, cell lifespan is strongly correlated with LMA reversibility, confirming that LMA reversibility is a decisive factor for achieving high cycling stability in a lean-electrolyte Li–S battery.

Additionally, in the DME electrolyte, a slight increase in discharge capacity was observed before degradation set in, likely due to LiPS dissolvoing out of the carbon structure and allowing reactions to occur on the outer carbon surface.
In contrast, in moderately solvating electrolytes, reactions were likely limited to the inner carbon surface, preventing such capacity increases (Figure S27, Supporting Information).

This behavior originates from the electron transfer to Li+, increasing the ease with which salt or solvent molecules are reduced.[32] Based on this consideration, in the DME electrolyte, the preferential participation of DME in the Li+ solvate will promote the cathodic decomposition of DME and enrich the organic components in the SEI.
In contrast, in the moderately solvating electrolytes, the involvement of the anions in the Li+ solvate may facilitate the cathodic decomposition of the anions, forming an inorganic-rich SEI.
The addition of the FE cosolvents to the DME electrolyte notably reduced the carbon content by over 25% within the SEI, and the DME-TFTFE electrolyte exhibited the lowest carbon content (Figure 5b).
This indicates substantial suppression of DME decomposition, as anticipated.

The abnormally high F content in the SEI in the DME-ETFE electrolyte can be explained by the low cathodic stability of ETFE owing to the localized electron distribution in this asymmetric structure.[33] As the NO3 −anion coordinated to Li+ is particularly susceptible to decomposition owing to the lowest LUMO level, we examined the N 1s spectra of the SEIs in the DME, DME-ETFE, DME- BTFE, and DME-TFTFE electrolytes (Figure 5c–f, respectively).

Moreover, the S 2p spectra of the SEIs (Figure S28, Supporting Information) displayed that the intensities corresponding to the LiPSs and Li2S in the DME-FE electrolytes were significantly lower than those in the DME electrolyte, evidencing the suppressed Li corrosion owing to the LiPSs in the moderately solvating electrolytes.
Overall, the compositional analysis validated the formation of inorganic-enriched SEIs and the mitigation of Li corrosion owing to the moderately solvating electrolytes.

The DME-BTFE and DME-TFTFE electrolytes exhibited more uniform Li-surface and cross-sectional morphologies than the DME and DME-ETFE electrolytes, in good agreement with the distinguished cycling stabilities of these electrolytes (Figure 4b).

Because electrolyte decomposition is aggravated owing to an inhomogeneous Li-deposit morphology, the uniform Li morphology driven by the DME-BTFE and DME-TFTFE electrolytes is beneficial for achieving high reversibility of the LMA.
The abnormally low remaining Li capacity of the DME-ETFE electrolyte can be attributed to the high chemical corrosion of Li by ETFE.
As demonstrated earlier, capacity drop during cycling is directly associated with electrolyte depletion.

The smaller FSI−retentions in the DME-ETFE and DME-BTFE electrolytes than that in the DME electrolyte indicate the preferential decomposition of the anion owing to increased anion coordination (decreased LUMO level of FSI- from Li+ coordination).
However, the DME-TFTFE electrolyte exhibited higher FSI−retention due to reduced Li corrosion, which is attributed to a more Adv.

This uniform Li-deposition in the DME-TFTFE electrolyte reduces the exposed surface area of the Li metal, resulting in less decomposition of DME, FSI−, and the FE cosolvent compared to other electrolytes.
Additionally, the ETFE cosolvent was nearly depleted after 36 cycles, indicating its poor cathodic stability.

As shown in Figure S19 (Supporting Information), the residual solvent quantities increased in the following order: DME-ETFE < DME < DME-BTFE < DME-TFTFE, strongly correlating with the order of their lifespans (Figure S31, Supporting Information).

Owing to substantial electrolyte loss, the DME electrolyte displayed a distorted lower voltage plateau at the 36th cycle (Figure S32a, Supporting Information), and the DME-ETFE electrolyte did not exhibit a lower voltage plateau at the corresponding Adv.

Notably, the DME-TFTFE electrolyte effectively mitigated electrolyte depletion, the root cause of cell failure, thereby enabling the stable operation of a pouch-type stack cell with a high cell-level energy density of 405 Wh kg−1 and stable cycling for 80 cycles at a Adv.

Our findings demonstrate that controlling the solvation structure through the interaction between DME and FE is a promising strategy to prevent electrolyte depletion due to Li corrosion, while maintaining the rapid redox kinetics of LiPSs under lean-electrolyte conditions.

We can identify a few trends in the measured Li+ solvation energies of different electrolytes.
First, as salt concentration increases, we observe a more positive solvation energy that corresponds to weaker solvation.

Second, mixtures of 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME) and 1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl-2,2,3,3-tetrafluoropropyl ether (TTE) solvents show that greater amounts of TTE leads to weaker (more positive) solvation free energies.

Third, the solvation strength of solvents increases in the order of 1,3-dioxolane (DOL)-DME-tetraethylene glycol dimethyl ether (G4), which is in agreement with previous reports in the literature19,25,26.

By employing a fluorinated−glyme (F-glyme) cosolvent, specifically 1,2-bis(2,2-difluoroethoxy)ethane (F4DEE), that exhibits low LiPS solubility yet moderate Li+ solvation, we designed an electrolyte that enhances lithium anode stability while maintaining sufficient sulfur cathode kinetics, thereby prolonging Li−S cell cycle life.

In contrast, solvation refers to the molecular-level interactions between the solute and the solvent molecules (Figure S1).24 An example for this distinction is that LiPS dimers and clusters exhibit high solubility but are weakly solvated in many solvents.21−23 Therefore, the design of advanced electrolytes requires decoupling the solubility and solvation of LiPS and Li+ to accelerate sulfur redox kinetics and enhance Li anode stability concurrently.

Overall, the DOL/F4DEE electrolyte balances sulfur cathode kinetics and lithium anode stability through optimized Li+ and LiPS solubility and solvation, thereby extending the cycle life of both Li−S coin cells and Li−S cells under more demanding cycling conditions (Figures S35 and S36).

Moreover, the retarded LiPS-S8 oxidation accelerates the irreversible consumption of LiNO3.50,51 This is unfavorable for Li−S long-term cycling because LiNO3 is crucial in SEI formation and catalyzing LiPS oxidation.52 Taking these into consideration, weak LiPS solvation in DOL/F4DEE benefits the Li−S battery cycle life despite partially compromised specific capacity.
In general, the weak LiPS solvation in DOL/F4DEE manifests remarkable influence on LiPS redox conversion (Figure S21), leading to the trade-off between capacity and cell cycle life.

Lithium salt concentration and Li+ solvation in the electrolyte determine Li stability by influencing Li+ transfer and Li solid-electrolyte interface (SEI).4 Li+ conductivity increases with LiTFSI concentration but will reach the peak value because high LiTFSI concentration impairs Li+ solvation and hinders Li+ transport.30 Moreover, high LiTFSI concentration inhibits LiPS dissolution by suppressing LiPS dissociation equilibrium (namely, the common-ion effect), resulting in low sulfur utilization.31 Hence, the LiTFSI concentration was optimized to be 1.0 M (Note S2).

Li+ solubility and solvation primarily dictate the electrolyte’s ionic conductivity and the reversibility of lithium anode stripping/plating.
In contrast, LiPS solvation governs the thermodynamics of sulfur (S8), LiPS, and lithium sulfide (Li2S) interconversion, while the LiPS solubility determines their redox kinetics.

Electrolytes play a pivotal role in Li−S battery performance by governing the Li anode and LiPS conversion through controlling the solubility and solvation of Li+ and LiPS.4,7 Conventional ether-based electrolytes, such as 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) and 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME),4 typically exhibit high lithium salt and LiPS solubility with strong Li+ and LiPS solvation.

While this supports ionic conductivity, it leads to severe LiPS shuttle and parasitic reactions on the lithium anode, limiting cycle life.8,9 To address this, sparely solvating electrolytes (SSEs) have been developed by adding nonsolvating cosolvents −often fluorinated ethers (F-ethers) −to DOL and DME, including compounds like 1,1,2,2-tetrafluoro- 3-(1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyoxy)propane (TTE),10,11 bis(2,2,2- trifluoroethyl) ether (BTFE),12 and octafluoropentyl-1,1,2,2- tetrafluoroethyl ether (OFE).13 The approach suppresses LiPS dissolution that mitigates the shuttle effect, and forms a fluorine-rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) on the Li anode,10,13,14 which helps regulate plating/stripping.

In extreme cases, the redox mechanism shifts to a sluggish quasi-solid-state sulfur conversion pathway that requires elevated temperatures.15,16 Additionally, the high viscosity of these electrolytes can cause poor electrode wetting, especially with high sulfur-loading cathodes.17 Despite these advances, achieving an optimal balance between lithium anode stability and fast sulfur redox kinetics remains a challenge.18−20 Li+ and LiPS exhibit distinct behaviors in Li−S electrolytes: LiPS tends to cluster, while lithium salts such as lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl) imide (LiTFSI) dissociate into Li+ cations and TFSI− anions.21−23 Furthermore, it is important to distinguish solvation and solubility, because they describe different physiochemical processes.
In addition to high Li+ conductivity, the moderate Li+ solvation in DOL/F4DEE enhances the Li stripping/plating stability.

Figure 2a and Figure S10 show Li stripping/plating Coulombic efficiency (CE) with varied Li+ solvation measured by Aurbach method in Li||Cu cells.32 Electrolytes with weaker Li+ solvation generally deliver higher CE.

The moderate Li+ solvation in DOL/F4DEE also regulates the stripping/ plating process of the Li anode, showing chunky and dense Li deposition morphology with a relatively reduced Li thickness (Figure 2b, Figure S11).

Such a morphology reduces the exposed interface area between the Li metal and the electrolyte, suppressing parasitic reactions for high CE.33 These results demonstrate the correlation between moderate Li+ solvation and improved Li stripping/plating reversibility in DOL/F4DEE, which aligns well with previous studies on the Li metal anode.18,19,34 The improved stability of the Li anode in the DOL/F4DEE electrolyte is further validated by its superior CE during long-term Li||Cu stripping/plating cycling (Figure S12).

In general, the weak LiPS solvation in DOL/F4DEE manifests remarkable influence on LiPS redox conversion (Figure S21), leading to the trade-off between capacity and cell cycle life.

Although DOL/F4DEE delivers lower capacity because of limited liquid−liquid reduction (stage II) and retarded solid−liquid oxidation (on stage IV), it leverages more on liquid−solid reduction (on stage III) and promotes liquid−solid oxidation (on stage V) to offset the capacity.

The combination of both tailored cell components would confine LiPS within the cathode, maximizing sulfur utilization, reducing the loss of active material, and extending cell cyclability.

However, KB-0.3rGO cells showed limited cyclability of around 30 cycles due to the combination of the high sulfur loading with the elevated solubility of lithium polysulfides in the DME/DOL electrolyte.
This salt creates a Lix- NOy-rich SEI layer on top of the lithium metal anode, and when LiNO3 is exhausted, the lithium metal surface is exposed and subsequently corroded leading to cell failure.
The larger the sulfur content in the cathode, the more stress the anode suffers and the faster the cell degrades.

In the novel DOL/OCTO SSE, OCTO was selected as a diluent because of its high fluorination degree and low LiPS dissolution ability [63], due to its weakened solvating power that results in a higher ratio of cation-anion aggregates (AGGs), as proven by Wang et al.

Aliphatic ethers such as DME with high donor numbers increase the LiPS solubility due to their Lewis basicity [40], which makes them not the most suitable candidate to prevent the polysulfide shuttle.
This might be due to the fact that DOL partially dissolves lithium polysulfides [67], which could be beneficial to a certain extent for accelerating their conversion reactions.

This test also demonstrates that the OCTO co-solvent impedes the polysulfide dissolution, and the combined effect obtained between DOL and OCTO in this SSE is promising in terms of restraining the polysulfide shuttle as well as accelerating the redox kinetics of the system.

The reduced ionic conductivity of the latter is intrinsic to the SSE family of compounds, where lithium-ion mobility is restricted, and this is reflected in a lower ionic conductivity of the electrolyte.

The larger ability of DME/DOL electrolyte to dissolve lithium polysulfides represents a drawback for the system, whereas the limited polysulfide dissolution in the DOL/OCTO electrolyte is beneficial for cell stability.

Regarding the previously discussed results achieved with DME/DOL, DOL/OCTO clearly outperforms the overall behavior of the classic ether-electrolyte offering higher discharge capacities and more stable electrochemical performance due to the excellent compatibility with the electrode and the reduced shuttle effect previously demonstrated.

Rather, due to the weakly solvating nature of this electrolyte demonstrated in the polysulfide dissolution tests, the presence of some polysulfide species is evidenced by the potential well occurring between plateaus, whose intensity increases upon cycling.
Hydrofluoroethers such as OCTO have a low donor ability [42,69, 70], which results in a low but non-negligible solubility of polysulfides.

As reported for other SSE, this type of electrolyte promotes the formation of medium or short-chain lithium polysulfides (Li2S4) compared to the long chain polysulfide species such as Li2S8 and Li2S6 favored in the conventional DME/DOL electrolyte, thus tuning the reaction pathway of lithium-sulfur discharge process.
The different voltage profiles for each electrolyte can be tentatively ascribed to this fact, although a deeper analysis is needed to confirm it.

Regarding the overvoltage between charge and discharge plateaus, in the first cycles it is higher in the case of the SSE electrolyte, but after 33 cycles the overvoltage of DME/DOL increases when LiNO3 is exhausted and Li0 unprotected, whereas in DOL/OCTO the overvoltage in the first cycle at C/10 and the 100th cycle is almost the same, demonstrating an effective reduction of the polysulfide shuttle.
Concerning the DME/DOL cell, besides the lightyellow coloration of the separator due to some polysulfide dissolution, the anode surface is clearly damaged.

In the SEM micrographs, there are no clear evidences of the positive electrode surface degradation, whereas the surface of lithium metal clearly shows mossy structures, pointing out to the uncontrolled and heterogeneous lithium growth during plating, with possible corrosion coming from the polysulfide reactivity with the anode, which could eventually lead to a prompt cell failure.

Opposite to this behavior, lithium deposition using DOL/OCTO electrolyte is smooth and homogeneous across all the Li0 surface, with the KB-0.3rGO cathode showing the same behavior as for the DME/DOL Fig. 6.

The higher salt concentration together with the lower polysulfide solubility and the nature of the diluent in the SSE allow for a homogeneous fluorine-rich SEI layer and a better plating/stripping behavior for the lithium metal anode.
Besides, the off-white color of the separator membrane soaked in DOL/OCTO further demonstrates that the polysulfide shuttle has been clearly reduced in comparison with the DME/DOL-based cells.

Characterization and calculation.—The viscosity was measured by viscometer (TV-35, TOKI SANGYO) equipped with a thermostat.
The viscosity of the electrolyte is found to be increasing as increasing the salt concentration.
For example, the values of viscosity at 298 K for pure AMImTFSI, 1 M LiTFSI, 2 M LiTFSI and 3 M LiTFSI in AMImTFSI are 30.1, 76.0, 236.4 and 664.0 mPa·s, respectively.

The ionic conductivity was analyzed by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) technique in the frequency range from 1 MHz to 10 mHz with voltage amplitude of 10 mV and temperature range of 30 °C∼60 °C using an impedance analyzer (Solartron 1260).
The values of ionic conductivity with acceptable order of magnitude of 10−3 S·cm−1 are exhibited in all cases of electrolyte.
Among them, the highest ionic conductivity is found in the low concentration electrolyte with 1 M LiTFSI, while very close values are observed in the case of 2 M and 3 M LiTFSI in AMImTFSI.

Unfortunately, at elevated temperatures (60 ◦C), both Li-S batteries using sulfolane electrolyte and DME/DOL electrolyte without LiNO3 additive exhibit the polysulfide shuttle effect, though to different ex­ tents, as shown in Fig. 1 (C) and 1 (D).

Consequently, the polysulfide shuttle effect in a Li-S battery with sulfolane electrolyte without LiNO3 was less severe than in a Li-S battery with DME/DOL electrolyte without LiNO3 even at elevated temperature.
In the case of the Li-S battery with DME/DOL electrolyte (without LiNO3), the shuttle effect is pronounced, preventing the battery from cycling from the start as shown in Fig. 1 (C).

For the Li-S battery with sulfolane electrolyte (without LiNO3), the shuttle effect becomes noticeable after 5 discharge/charge cycles (with about 10 % overcharging), and the battery fails to cycle after 35 discharge/charge cycles due to the severe and notorious shuttle effect as shown in Fig. 1 (D).

This high viscosity could be a reason for the different cycling performance observed: the sulfolane electrolyte might kineti­ cally slow down mass transfer due to its high viscosity thereby miti­ gating the polysulfide shuttle effect even without LiNO3 additive.
In contrast, the low viscosity of DME/DOL electrolyte could accelerate the mass transfer, promoting the polysulfide shuttle effect in the absence of LiNO3 additive.
One possible reason for this inhibition effect is the very high viscosity of sulfolane electrolyte, which could kinetically slow down the diffusion of polysulfides between cathode and lithium anode.
The results illustrated in Fig. 2 indicated that the polysulfide solution in the sulfolane electrolyte is less reactive with lithium metal compared to the polysulfide solution in DME/DOL electrolyte.

Both electrochemical cycling data (Fig. 1) and HPLC analysis (Fig. 2) indicate that the “polysulfide shuttle effect” in Li/S battery with sulfo­ lane electrolyte is minimized, if not eliminated, even without LiNO3 additive.

The results clearly showed that when the sulfolane to DME volume ratio decreased to 7:3, the polysulfide shuttle effect emerged and negatively impacted the performance of Li-S battery.
Fundamentally, the poly­ sulfide shuttle phenomenon originates from the thermodynamically favorable reaction between lithium metal and long-chain polysulfides.
This makes the shuttle phenomenon inevitable, and can only be miti­ gated through kinetic approaches as demonstrated in numerous studies on Li-S batteries with nonaqueous liquid electrolytes [4–7].
However, the shuttle effect for Li-S battery with sulfolane electrolyte without LiNO3 was more pronounced than in those using sulfolane electrolyte with LiNO3.
It is likely due to the different SEI compositions on Li metal surfaces for sulfolane electrolyte with and without LiNO3 as demonstrated by the study of SEI composition in DME/DOL electrolytes. 4.

greatly reduced the reactivity between Li metal and polysulfides, even at elevated temperature as shown in Fig. 2 (D) and 2 (H).
Additionally, the difference in the SEI composition on lithium anode surface could also contribute to this effect.

However, at elevated tem­ perature, which thermodynamically and kinetically favors the poly­ sulfide shuttle, a severe polysulfide shuttle effect was observed in the Li- S batteries with sulfolane electrolyte without LiNO3.
Only when LiNO3 is added to the sulfolane electrolyte can the polysulfide shuttle effect be effectively mitigated at higher temperature in a Li-S battery.
